name: Clean Break
beta: The route is characterized by sustained hand crack climbing through the first ten pitches, with notable splitter cracks throughout. Pitches 11-15 step down to mid-5th class terrain and can be simul-climbed from a ledge system. Route-finding requires care on the lower pitches in the talus approach section.
overview: Clean Break rises 1,500 feet above the valley floor on the steep east buttress of Juno Tower, named for the long rock scar left on pitch 2. With several of its 15 pitches at 5.10, this sustained granite route is regarded as one of the finest long multi-pitch climbs at this grade in Washington.

current.approach: Park at the pullout where SR-20 crosses Silver Star Creek near milepost 171, about 8.5 miles east of Washington Pass. A good climbers' trail follows the east side of the creek for a couple of miles, then crosses it and climbs talus and forest up the western edge of the valley toward Juno Tower; at about 5,000 ft a rising traverse leftward threads most of the slide alder to the foot of the east prow. The usual way down is the Burgundy Col trail to the Wine Spires pullout near milepost 166, farther west on the highway: from Burgundy Col (~7,720 ft) it drops to a basin/camp bench around 6,500 ft (good camping and a late-season spring near 6,400-6,500 ft), descends the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, crosses Early Winters Creek on a log (~4,080 ft) past a trail register, and climbs a short loose talus/scree slope back up to the road. Walking up the east side of Silver Star Creek from the pullout is mostly simple open cross-country to the base, with little bushwhacking if you pick your line.
approach_variant_names: Silver Star Creek to the east prow of Juno Tower
current.descent: Two descent options exist: (1) From the summit, traverse south toward Bench Camp below Burgundy Col; this takes approximately 1 hour to reach Bench Camp. From Bench Camp, follow the established trail down to Highway 20 (approximately 1 hour more), then hitch-hike back to the vehicle. (2) Alternatively, scramble northwest to Sunset Col and descend the Sunset Col trail back toward Silver Star Creek drainage, rejoining the approach route.
current.detailed_rack: Bring a full set of nuts in all sizes and doubles of cams from #0.75 to #3. A #4 cam is useful for pitches 6-7 (the #4 once left fixed on P7 is gone; bring your own). A single 60m rope is enough, since the descent is a walk-off.
current.pro_needs: Climbers must be proficient with hand and finger crack protection placement. Solid experience on multi-pitch alpine routes at this grade and comfort with route-finding in semi-wild terrain is essential.
bivy: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
current.rope_note: IV, 1500ft, 15-pitch splitter-crack route on Juno Tower's east buttress; several pitches are 5.10. The descent is a walk-off, so a single 60m rope is enough.

name: Cobbles 101
beta: Ground-up bolted route established by Jim Yoder and Brenden Sullivan; 5 pitches of sustained 5.6–5.8 climbing on knobby, cobble-textured welded-tuff breccia, including a hand traverse and a stepped 'spine' feature, finishing through the same basalt band and summit chute as Bowling Alley.
overview: A harder, more sustained 5-pitch sport line up the prow just left of the Bowling Alley gully, climbing a distinctive 'cobblestone staircase' of knobs to the same summit exit.

current.approach: From the NF-77 pullout, a well-used trail runs along the base of the formation. The West Face and North Side are different aspects of the same rock reached via short spurs off this main trail, generally under 15 minutes' walk from the parking pullout.
current.descent: From the top, move to the rappel anchor near a tree at the north end of the formation. With a single 60m rope, two rappels down bolted anchors return climbers to the base; with two ropes, one long rappel suffices. Tie stopper knots in the rope ends — the rappels can otherwise run the ends off the rock.
current.detailed_rack: 12 quickdraws total, mixing standard draws with a few longer alpine draws for the P2/P3 traverse and link-up to reduce rope drag; no trad gear is used.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted to chain/fixed anchors on every pitch — bring a standard set of 10–12 quickdraws plus a couple of alpine draws for the traversing sections. No trad rack required.
current.rope_note: Pinto Rock South Face, 5 pitches, knobby rock ('cobbletrust' skill-building route); bolted throughout, with an occasional knob or cobble to sling.

name: West Face
beta: The West Face is one of the best sustained alpine rock routes in the North Cascades, offering nearly 1000 feet of climbing with memorable pitches including an enduro corner, wild roof traverse, protected crux, and the region's hardest 5.8 chimney. The route culminates in an exposed V1 boulder problem topping out the balanced rock. Traditional protection is required throughout with natural gear placements and in-situ slings for rappel anchors.
overview: A striking detached granite tower perched above Colchuck Lake near Dragontail Peak, Colchuck Balanced Rock's West Face is regarded as one of the best 5.10-and-up multipitch rock climbs in the North Cascades: roughly 850-1000 vertical feet over 9 pitches of clean granodiorite, with an enduro corner, a wild roof traverse, a short, well-protected 5.11+/5.12- crux, and what many call the region's hardest 5.8 (a flaring chimney pitch). The route tops out with a short V1 boulder problem to reach the nested summit block. First climbed by Tom Boley and Jack Lewis in 1980; Nathan Farr and Blake Herrington made the first winter ascent in late January 2012, climbing it in gloves and oversized rock shoes over snow-covered rock.

current.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601, off Icicle Creek Road outside Leavenworth; NW Forest Pass required). Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) about 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge around the 1.5-mile mark, to the signed junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) splits left. Continue on #1599A, crossing Mountaineer Creek again on a second log bridge, then climb increasingly steep, rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain from the trailhead, roughly 1:45-2:00 for a fit party with a rack). From the lake there are two ways into the west basin below Colchuck Balanced Rock (CBR): the shorter northern line crosses the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follows a climbers' path across a timbered hillside directly into the cirque below the west face (about an hour, plus roughly 20-25 minutes of boulder-hopping to the actual base); the longer southern/Aasgard option follows the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, cuts north through a band of slide alder (look for cairns), then climbs the leftmost gully about 1,000 ft to its top before contouring east on an easy path into the basin (1.5-2 hours total, more elevation gain but avoids the outlet ford). Colchuck Lake is the last reliable water; the basin and route itself are dry. Hazards: the Mountaineer Creek log-bridge crossings can be slick or partially submerged in high early-season flow, the slide-alder section is a genuine bushwhack, the gully and basin talus are loose, and snow can linger in the gully well into early summer, making an ice axe/traction useful before mid-July.
approach_variant_names: Lake outlet climbers' path into the west cirque
Southern line via the Aasgard-side slopes and the leftmost gully
current.descent: Descend the same way you climbed the upper pitches: from the top, scramble to a slung horn on the east side of the summit block and make one roughly 30-meter (about 100 ft) rappel — a single rope is sufficient, though some parties extend it with a doubled 60m for a lower touchdown. The anchor is a natural horn wrapped in webbing rather than bolts, so back it up or add your own sling if it looks tired; it sees heavy traffic and gets re-slung periodically. From the rappel's end, downclimb/scramble sandy scree and talus, working rightward (clockwise around the peak, roughly south then west) back into the basin and to your pack stash at the base of the west face — about 45 minutes to an hour car-to-base-equivalent. Some parties skip the rappel entirely and downclimb the same easy scree/snow line if conditions allow, since the terrain below the horn is low-angle. No further rappels are needed; this is the standard, single-rappel descent used for the West Face, The Scoop, and other CBR lines that top out on the summit block.
current.detailed_rack: A double rack to 3.5 inches with extra mid-size cams (0.5-2 inch) covers the crack systems well; bring a single 60m rope for the descent rappel.
current.pro_needs: Steady gear placements throughout on well-featured cracks and corners; the crux roof/hand-crack pitch protects well but is strenuous and exposed.

name: Colchuck Glacier
beta: Beckey's 'East Route,' almost universally known today as the Colchuck Glacier Route. From the base of the glacier, ascend easy snow on the left (east) lobe past the base of Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone Ridge routes. The angle increases near the Colchuck-Dragontail saddle to roughly 100 ft of 40-degree snow, then eases into 3rd-class sandy scrambling to the 8,500 ft summit plateau and on to the true 8,705 ft summit. With good snow cover it's an easy 3-4 hour climb from a camp at Colchuck Lake, or is readily done car-to-car in a long day.
overview: The Colchuck Glacier (Beckey's 'East Route') is the classic, most-climbed line on Colchuck Peak: an easy-angled snow/glacier ascent up the peak's northeast side to the Colchuck-Dragontail col, then a short 3rd-class scramble to the summit. From the north shore of Colchuck Lake, climbers gain the crest of the lateral moraine early to avoid loose scree, then move onto the glacier's left (east) lobe, passing below Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone Ridge. The glacier steepens to roughly 100 ft of 40-degree snow just below the Colchuck-Dragontail saddle; above the col, sandy 3rd-class steps lead to a broad summit plateau around 8,500 ft, and the true summit (8,705 ft) is a short walk west/north from there.

current.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FS Road 7601, Eightmile Road, ~3,400 ft — reached via Icicle Road/FS 76 from Leavenworth, roughly 8.4 miles, then FS 7601 another 3.8 miles), follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 south along Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles/1,100 ft of gain to the signed fork; take the right/south branch (Colchuck Lake Trail) and climb steep switchbacks through boulders for another 1.6 miles/1,100 ft to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, about 4 miles and 2,200 ft from the trailhead — a popular, often-permitted overnight zone in the Enchantments quota area, so many parties camp here rather than pushing to the summit car-to-car). Colchuck Lake is the last reliable water. From the lake, follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail and climb talus (or snow early season) directly up the basin toward the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600–6,800 ft — this is the standard, moderate line up the peak (3rd class/mod. snow) and doubles as the descent for the other two routes here. The glacier itself is not significantly crevassed but is frequently icy by mid-to-late season, so crampons and an axe (and a rope if any crevasses/moats have opened) are standard; stay right of the main rockfall line coming off the surrounding faces, especially in the morning-warming window. Ascend the glacier to Colchuck–Dragontail Col (Colchuck Col/Banshee Pass, ~8,200 ft), then scramble northwest on blocky terrain to the summit (8,705 ft).
approach_variant_names: Colchuck Lake, snow-covered glacier (early season)
Colchuck Lake, bare-ice glacier (late season)
current.descent: This is a walk-off — no rappels. Reverse the ascent line: descend the glacier (staying climber's left, away from the thin crevasse zone that has opened as the glacier has retreated) and back down the lateral moraine to Colchuck Lake, then follow the Colchuck Lake Trail and Stuart Lake Trail back to the trailhead. In early season with good snow cover, much of the glacier and the upper trail basin can be glissaded, which many parties use to save time — but glissading here carries the usual runout/collision risk of any steep snow slope, so glissade only with a self-arrest-ready ice axe and clear runout. By afternoon on warm days the glacier softens considerably (postholing, wet-slide potential on any residual snow slopes), so climbers doing this as a long day often aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon.
current.detailed_rack: A 30 to 60m glacier rope and a couple of pickets. No rock gear is needed for the standard line.
rack: 30-60m glacier rope for a 2-person rope team
Crevasse-rescue kit (pulley, prusiks, screw-gate biners) per rope team
current.pro_needs: Protection is limited to pickets in the steeper snow near the col and standard glacier-travel anchors. The summit rocks are low-class scrambling and take no gear.
bivy: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
current.rope_note: A short 30m rope is standard for a 2-person rope team crossing this glacier; parties only extend to 60m if a larger group is roping together or pitching out the steeper snow near the col.

name: North Buttress Couloir
beta: From the far side of Colchuck Lake, hike uphill to gain the moraine, follow it to the right, and drop into the large couloir at the edge of the Colchuck Glacier. In winter and early season it is continuous snow the entire way; later in summer, Class 4 rock can be exposed in a few short steps. The route can be climbed minimalist and fast, or fully protected with rock gear, pickets, and screws. Descent is via the Colchuck Glacier route on the peak's far side.
overview: The most direct couloir rising out of the Colchuck Glacier's moraine on Colchuck Peak's north side — a popular introduction to steep snow and easy mixed climbing, with conditions ranging from a straightforward snow slog to thin mixed rock-and-ice.

current.approach: Follow the shared Colchuck Peak approach: from Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road ~8.4 mi to FR 7601, then FR 7601 ~3.7 mi to Stuart Lake Trailhead; hike the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trail (~4-4.5 mi, ~2,200 ft gain) to Colchuck Lake. From the lake's far (south) side, hike up and gain the moraine, follow it to the right, and drop into the couloir — it is the first major gully reached rising out of the toe of the Colchuck Glacier's moraine.
approach_variant_names: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
current.descent: Descend the backside of the mountain onto the Colchuck Glacier and follow its standard route and the moraine back to Colchuck Lake; in soft, late-day snow this descent has been reported as slow and exhausting.
current.detailed_rack: Two pickets, two ice screws (14-22 cm), a small cam rack (roughly 0.5-2 in) and a few small pitons/nuts covers most conditions; parties climbing fast and light often carry little to no gear.
current.pro_needs: Protection needs scale with conditions: firm early-season snow wants pickets and screws, while a thinner, mixed/rock finish later in the season wants a light rock rack.

name: Northeast Couloir
beta: Follow the couloir off the Colchuck Glacier as it winds upward and steepens; the gully hits a steep wall, so continue along the base of this wall to climber's left to find the exit, finishing on steep snow/ice to 60+ degrees that gains the summit ridge. Protection is a mix of snow gear and a small alpine rock rack including pitons. It is usually rated roughly Grade II with an elevation gain of about 1,500 ft from the glacier to the ridge; some grade it up to Grade III depending on conditions.
overview: The Northeast Couloir splits off about a third of the way up the Colchuck Glacier and climbs the shaded northeast flank of the peak on firm snow and short ice steps, with a steeper entry and exit — reported up to 60 degrees — that deposits climbers on the ridge just below the summit. It's sometimes used as a less committing alternative when Dragontail's Triple Couloirs are out of condition, but it still demands solid steep-snow/ice technique and good avalanche judgment, since it's a confined, shaded gully.

current.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FS Road 7601 (Eightmile Road), elevation ~3,400 ft — in early season when Eightmile Road is gated/snowed in, tack on roughly 4 additional miles of road walking/skiing from the Bridge Creek Campground area on Icicle Road. From the trailhead, follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 south along Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles and 1,100 ft of gain to the signed junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail forks left; the Stuart Lake Trail continues straight to Stuart Lake/Colchuck Pass and is not your route. Climb the steep, rooty switchbacks of the Colchuck Lake Trail through boulder fields for another 1.6 miles and 1,100 ft to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4 miles and 2,200 ft from the car) — this is the only reliable water source below the basin, and it's your last easy resupply. Follow the trail and boot path along the lake's west shore to the inlet at the south end (~5 miles in). Leave the maintained trail here and ascend talus, heather benches, or lingering snow (highly season-dependent) up the basin toward the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600–6,800 ft. Rather than heading up-glacier toward Colchuck/Banshee Col (that's the Colchuck Glacier route), traverse along the glacier's true-right (climber's right) margin toward Colchuck Peak's north side, staying well right of the main fall line under the north face and Northeast Buttress to limit rockfall and icefall exposure. The Northeast Couloir's entrance is the obvious narrow slot higher up the glacier than the North Buttress Couloir, directly below the Northeast Buttress; gaining it typically requires crossing a moat at the glacier's edge, which varies from a simple step-across in early season to an awkward downclimb by mid-to-late summer. Expect avalanche-prone slopes above the lake in spring/early-summer conditions, and increasing rockfall down the couloir itself as the day warms.
approach_variant_names: Colchuck Lake and the true-right margin of the Colchuck Glacier
current.descent: Standard descent is the walk-off: from the summit, traverse/downclimb to the Colchuck–Dragontail col (Colchuck Col, also called Banshee Pass) and descend the Colchuck Glacier's east/true-right lobe back to the basin above Colchuck Lake, then reverse the approach trail — the same line used to descend the Colchuck Glacier route. This is the recommended way down; reversing through the Northeast Couloir itself is discouraged because of loose rock in the entry gully and awkward mixed downclimbing. That said, some parties (particularly ski descents or parties that got benighted) do reverse the couloir instead of the full glacier walk-off: accounts describe downclimbing back to the top of the upper rock band, then either downclimbing it (not recommended) or making a single ~50m rappel off a natural anchor (you'll likely need to build one from boulders/slings — nothing fixed is documented) down to a ledge system on the southeast face; from there, a gully just east of the couloir's top can be down-climbed or rappelled with two or three single-strand 30m raps (again on natural/rigged anchors) to reach easier snow slopes, from which you continue down into the basin. Treat this as an emergency/alternate option, not the primary plan. No rappels are needed on the standard Colchuck Glacier walk-off descent; the main hazards there are a possible moat step-across near the col and glissade-glazed or icy snow by midsummer.
current.detailed_rack: A handful of ice screws including a stubby or two, a couple of pickets, two technical tools per climber, a small rock rack for the exit, and a 60m rope for protecting steep steps and retreat.
rack: Small cam set to 2in + small nuts for the rock exit
60m rope (some parties carry 2x50m for full-length raps)
current.pro_needs: Snow takes pickets; the ice steps take screws where the ice is thick enough. Rock protection at the exit is intermittent, so be ready for some thin or runout climbing through the cornice.
bivy: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
current.rope_note: A single 60m rope lets parties link the moderate snow sections into fewer, longer pitches and provides enough length to build picket/rock rappel anchors on the steeper ice steps and rock exit; some parties instead carry 2x50m ropes to allow full-length raps off the crux exit.

name: Cosley-Houston Couloir
beta: Approach via the Coleman Glacier to the base of Colfax Peak's north face. Start just above the bergschrund with a low-angle ice ramp trending up to the base of the crux pillar. The crux pillar is short and steep, slightly overhung, with approximately 30-40 feet of dead vertical or slightly overhanging water ice. After the crux, continue up a steep snow gully trending right, then simul-climb upper snow slopes to the summit ridge. A working knowledge of ice screw placement and anchor construction is essential.
overview: Colfax Peak is one of the Black Buttes, eroded remnants of an older Mount Baker volcanic cone on Baker's northwest shoulder above the Coleman Glacier. The Cosley-Houston is the easiest of Colfax's steep north-face ice lines: a meandering ~600 ft, 4-pitch WI4 route that starts just above the bergschrund with a low-angle ice ramp to a short, near-vertical crux pillar, then follows a gully system up and right through mixed ground to the summit ridge. It's a popular cold-weather testpiece, often in condition from late October into May.

current.approach: From the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (~3,700 ft, end of Glacier Creek Road/FR 39), follow the Heliotrope Ridge Trail (#677) through forest for roughly 2 miles, crossing a plank bridge over Grouse Creek and one avalanche-path/rockfall gully below Hogsback that can hold hazardous debris and running water in warm conditions. The trail breaks out of trees near a viewpoint of Coleman Glacier icefall around 4,900-5,000 ft; this is the last reliable running water before the moraine. From there, gain the lateral moraine and the well-worn Coleman-Deming boot track (the standard Mount Baker route), staying on or near the crest of the moraine before dropping onto glacier ice. Rope up for glacier travel here — crevasse hazard is real and grows through the season. Contour/ascend the Coleman Glacier heading climber's right (northeast) toward the prominent bench/rognon beneath the north faces of Colfax Peak, staying low and left around a well-known large crevasse that guards the direct line; parties commonly reach this bench in 3 to 4.5 hours from the car with good booting conditions, slower after new snow or when the skin track has been chewed up by skiers. Total gain to the route base near 8,000 ft is on the order of 4,500-4,700 ft over roughly 4-5 miles one-way; the upper glacier and bergschrund crossing should be done early before the north-facing slopes see any sun-warming, and this route/aspect avalanches after new snow, so avoid climbing after significant snowfall or in elevated avalanche danger.
approach_variant_names: Heliotrope Ridge Trail #677 and the Coleman Glacier to the bench beneath the north faces
current.descent: Cosley-Houston is a walk-off, not a rappel descent. From the summit area, follow the boot track (or break a new one) toward Colfax's secondary/eastern summit, then contour around its south side just below the top — no technical downclimbing is required on a normal-conditions descent. This drops you to the Colfax-Baker col (the Baker-Colfax saddle). From the saddle, pick up the standard Coleman-Deming route down the Coleman Glacier, roping up again and watching for the same crevasses navigated on the way up (some parties note trending to the glacier's right side to find solid bridges late-season). Continue down to the moraine, then the Heliotrope Ridge Trail back to the trailhead. Give yourself a real daylight margin for this: parties specifically warn against descending the glacier after dark, and parties that summit late have ended up down-climbing the icy trail by headlamp. There is no rappelling on the standard descent.
current.detailed_rack: 60 m rope; 8-10 ice screws (most racked for the short crux pitch, including a couple of stubbies); a few pickets; a light rock rack (small cams/nuts, maybe a pin) for anchors in the poor-quality summit rock; V-thread hardware for a retreat.
current.pro_needs: 8-10 ice screws (concentrated on the crux pitch), a few pickets, and a light rock rack/pin for belay anchors in poor rock; V-thread hardware for a retreat.
bivy: Coleman Glacier bivy under the Black Buttes north faces

name: Ford's Theatre
beta: Occupies a hidden cleft on the right side of a buttress on the north face, offering three pitches of steep ice before the angle eases into steep snow gullies; the route finishes by joining the final ~100 ft of the Cosley-Houston Couloir to reach the summit. Belay options are limited after the opening pitch — an experienced party could consider combining the second and third pitches to avoid intermediate ice-screw anchors.
overview: A hidden line in a cleft on the right side of a buttress on Colfax's north face, climbing three pitches of steep ice before mellowing into snow gullies and finishing up the last stretch of the Cosley-Houston to the summit.

current.approach: Same as the Cosley-Houston and Polish Route: from Glacier, WA via Glacier Creek Road (FS-39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, up the Heliotrope Ridge Trail onto the Coleman Glacier moraine, then glacier travel to the base of Colfax's north face.
approach_variant_names: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then right around the buttress into the cleft
current.descent: Walk-off via the Coleman-Deming route (as for the Cosley-Houston, which this route joins near the top), no rappels.
current.detailed_rack: The first ascent party carried ten ice screws, snow pickets for belays and upper-snowfield protection, plus a small rock rack and pins that went unused.
current.pro_needs: Ice-screw protected on the three opening ice pitches; pickets protect the upper snow gullies and the shared finish with the Cosley-Houston.

name: Kimchi Suicide Volcano
beta: Climbs an independent line to the left of the Polish Route on Colfax's north face, following steep ice interspersed with rock steps that offer plentiful face holds, though protection isn't always straightforward. Regarded by its first ascensionists as one of the highest-quality alpine climbs they'd done in the Cascades, alongside the Cosley-Houston and Polish Route.
overview: An independent mixed line on Colfax's north face, just left of the Polish Route — the first route on the wall to be more of a true mixed climb than a pure ice line.

current.approach: Same as the Cosley-Houston and Polish Route: from Glacier, WA via Glacier Creek Road (FS-39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, up the Heliotrope Ridge Trail onto the Coleman Glacier moraine, then glacier travel to the base of Colfax's north face.
approach_variant_names: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then the leftmost line on the face
current.descent: The route finishes on easy snow and ice slopes to the summit of Colfax Peak, and the way down is a walk-off with no rappels. Cross the Colfax-Baker col behind the summit and pick up the standard Coleman-Deming route down the Coleman Glacier, as for the neighboring routes on this face. Stay roped for the glacier and expect the same crevasses you passed on the way in. Follow the lateral moraine to the Heliotrope Ridge Trail and the trailhead, and leave daylight for the glacier, since descending it late is slow and hazardous.
current.pro_needs: Mixed rock/ice protection; the first ascent party noted the rock offers plenty of face holds but that gear placements aren't always straightforward, warranting a small rock rack alongside screws.
bivy: Coleman Glacier bivy under the Black Buttes north faces

name: Polish Route
beta: Approach via Coleman Glacier to the base of Colfax Peak's north face, directly below the middle of the face. Ascend the initial bergschrund crossing (may require traversal from the right if overhanging). Pitch 1: Long pitch of WI4+ to a snow slope. Pitch 2 (crux): Steep ice for approximately 30 feet, easing briefly, then rising to a free-hanging ice dagger grading WI6. This is the technical and psychological crux requiring bold movement and precise tool placement. Above the dagger: additional steep ice steps in a right-side gully. Final pitches: Upper snowfield with occasional blue ice patches, traversing between rock buttresses to gain the summit snowfield.
overview: The Polish Route is widely regarded as the best line on Colfax's north face: a striking, direct ~1,000 ft, 4-pitch WI6 ice line running straight up the middle of the wall, culminating in a free-hanging ice dagger crux. It sits alongside the easier Cosley-Houston (WI4) and Ford's Theatre (WI4+) as one of the North Cascades' premier moderate-to-hard alpine ice objectives, best climbed cold with the dagger fully formed.

current.approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as Cosley-Houston: from the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (~3,700 ft) follow Trail #677 roughly 2 miles through forest (last reliable water near treeline/moraine) to the Coleman Glacier moraine, then join the standard Coleman-Deming boot track onto the glacier. Rope up for crevasse travel. Head climber's right toward the bench beneath Colfax's north face — parties leaving the car around 3:30 am in good conditions have reported reaching the bench in under 3 hours with a well-consolidated track, though this varies a lot with snowpack and traffic. From the bench, gear up and cross the bergschrund, which guards the Polish Route directly: it is frequently large and overhanging and has required climbers to traverse right and tunnel through overhanging snow/ice to gain the first ice pitch. The route climbs the obvious continuous ice line up the middle of Colfax's north face, just left of (and parallel to) the Cosley-Houston gully. Because the face is northwest-facing, it holds ice longest in the shade of an early start but catches afternoon sun, so climbing parties should be off the technical ground before then; this aspect also avalanches after new snow, so the bergschrund/lower-face approach should not be done after recent loading.
approach_variant_names: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then the schrund guarding the middle of the face
current.descent:
The way down is on foot, not by rappel: from the top, continue to the Colfax-Baker saddle and descend the Coleman Glacier, the same walk-off used from the neighbouring lines on this face.

Retreating from partway up is a different matter. A V-thread in the ice is the normal way off if you bail on or below the dagger pitch, so carry screws and cord for building fresh threads rather than trusting anything left behind; ice quality and thickness change through the season.

Going down, watch for the same crevasse hazards on the Coleman Glacier as on the approach, and budget enough daylight — the glacier descent in the dark is unpleasant and hazardous.
current.detailed_rack: 60 m rope; 10+ ice screws (several stubbies) concentrated for the WI6 crux pitch; V-thread/Abalakov hardware; a couple of pickets for the upper snowfield; extra slings/cord for tat at existing anchors.
current.pro_needs: 10+ ice screws weighted toward the WI6 crux pitch, V-thread/Abalakov hardware, and a couple of pickets for the upper snowfield; a rock rack is not typically needed.
bivy: Coleman Glacier bivy under the Black Buttes north faces

name: West Ridge / Colonial Glacier
beta: West Ridge via the Colonial Glacier. From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead on SR-20, follow the trail to Pyramid Lake, then a steep climbers' path up the forested rib to camps near the edge of the Colonial Glacier (~6,000 ft). Cross the glacier toward the Colonial-Snowfield col, gain the west ridge through a notch, and follow the exposed ridge (class 3-4 with short low-5th steps) to the summit; many parties rappel the summit block on descent. Crevasse hazard on the glacier; loose rock and exposure on the ridge. Ice axe, crampons, rope, and glacier kit required. Best July-September. No confirmed public GPS track for this route; navigation skills required.
overview: Colonial Peak is one of the steepest-rising summits in the North Cascades, gaining roughly 6,500+ ft above Diablo Lake's Thunder Arm in under 2.5 horizontal miles. It lies in the North Unit of North Cascades National Park, accessed through the Ross Lake National Recreation Area corridor along SR 20, and shares its glaciated basin with Snowfield Peak, Neve Peak, and Paul Bunyan's Stump — a popular multi-summit basin for Mountaineers-style basic glacier climbs. The standard route (sometimes called the West Ridge) climbs the Colonial Glacier on the northeast side to the Colonial-Snowfield col, then follows the ridge over talus and firn to a short, exposed class 3-4 summit block. First climbed July 31, 1931 by William Degenhardt and Herbert Strandberg.

current.approach: Start at the signed Pyramid Lake Trailhead on SR 20 (small pullout on the north side of the highway, ~21 miles east of Marblemount and just past the Diablo turnoff, elev. ~1,150 ft; no parking pass needed, NPS backcountry permit if camping). Follow the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail — a well-used boot path through second-growth and old-growth forest — which climbs a steady, unrelenting ~1,500-1,600 ft over about 2.1-2.3 miles to Pyramid Lake (~2,600 ft). This maintained-trail portion ends at the lake; everything above is climbers'-trail/off-trail travel. Pick up the boot path around the right (east/north) side of the lake and continue climbing, now through brush, heather, and talus, gaining roughly 2,000 more feet up onto the crest of Pyramid Ridge. A knoll around 5,400-5,500 ft on this ridge is the customary high camp/bivy — seasonal ponds and puddles here and near ~4,500 ft (reported dry by late summer in low-snow years) are the last reliable water before the glacier. From the ridge crest, follow the climbers' path along the ridge over several knolls toward the base of Pyramid Peak, then drop and traverse a mix of scree and boulder-hop terrain beneath Pyramid's crumbly north face to reach the flat 6,100 ft basin at the toe of the Colonial Glacier — this traverse is loose underfoot and exposed to rockfall from above, and is the route's main approach-specific hazard. From the glacier-toe basin, rope up for glacier travel and ascend the Colonial Glacier, trending southeast/east across the upper glacier (crevasses are usually well-bridged under seasonal snow but are present and have been reported as a hazard, along with cornices along the traverse toward the Colonial-Snowfield col that are invisible from camp below) to reach the Colonial-Snowfield col or the base of the historic Northeast Gully. From the col, leave the ice for a loose gully leading up onto the West Ridge, which is then followed via Class 3-4 rock scrambling to the summit horn. Total car-to-summit distance runs roughly 10-14 miles round trip (parties differ depending on camp placement) with the ~6,600 ft of gain split roughly evenly between the maintained trail, the ridge/scree traverse, and the glacier-to-summit push.
approach_variant_names: Pyramid Lake, the 5,800 ft notch, and the traverse to the glacier toe
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the east ridge back to the head of the Northeast Gully, then downclimb/plunge-step the snow gully back down to the Colonial-Snowfield col, drop back onto the Colonial Glacier, and retrace the rope-up glacier traverse and the loose scree/boulder traverse beneath Pyramid Peak back to the Pyramid Ridge camp, then follow the climbers' path and maintained Pyramid Lake Trail back to the car. This is fundamentally a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel-dependent descent — but on the class 3-4 rock near the summit ridge, trip reports document an existing rap station (a sling/webbing anchor around a rock horn, not bolted) that some parties use for a short single-rope rappel (roughly 20-30m, any single rope 30m+ works) over the steepest step; other parties simply downclimb this same section instead, since it's optional class 3-4 terrain for a confident scrambler. There is no other fixed or bolted rappel infrastructure reported on this route. Descent hazards mirror the approach in reverse: softening glacier snow and weaker crevasse bridges later in the day, loose rock in the gully and on the summit ridge scramble, potential rockfall on the Pyramid traverse, and the reported cornice hazard along the glacier traverse near the col — parties should time the glacier/col crossing for firm early-morning or evening snow rather than midday.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier travel kit (rope, pickets/screws as conditions dictate) plus a few small-to-mid cams/nuts and slings for the short class 4 summit step and the optional horn rappel; a 30m single rope is plenty.
current.pro_needs: Roped glacier travel with steep snow, then short exposed summit rock; minimal rock pro.
bivy: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col

name: Standard Scramble
beta: From a high camp at Twin Lakes (or Silver Lake near Poodle Dog Pass), climbers head cross-country toward Columbia Peak's west spur, working up boulder fields and heather benches onto the connecting ridge, staying low on the ridge rather than crossing its crest. A class 3 scramble leads to a roughly 5-ft class 4 chimney/crack move near a buttress, after which the route crosses onto the southwest face - slabby but increasingly loose rock higher up - before a final cliff band is bypassed via class 3 terrain to the summit. Sustained scrambling above the Twin Lakes saddle totals roughly 800 vertical feet. The peak is often linked with neighboring Monte Cristo Peak and Kyes Peak in a Monte Cristo-group traverse.
overview: Columbia Peak (7,172 ft) is a sharp, glacially-carved summit in the Monte Cristo group of the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, forming a cirque with neighboring Monte Cristo Peak and Kyes Peak (its line parent) that holds the Columbia Glacier and the popular, turquoise Blanca Lake below. The standard route — the West Spur, rated Grade I, Class 3-4 — is reached via the historic Monte Cristo ghost-town approach out of Barlow Pass: typically a long single day or, more commonly, an overnight camp at Twin Lakes, followed by an off-trail ridge traverse and a varied, blocky scramble with one exposed 4th-class move around 6,700-6,800 ft.

current.approach: From the Verlot Public Service Center, continue east on the (now fully paved) Mountain Loop Highway roughly 19.5 miles to the large Barlow Pass trailhead/parking area (permit required). From the parking lot, follow the old Monte Cristo mining road — gated to public vehicles — east for about 4 miles (roughly 500 ft of gentle gain); this stretch is popular to mountain-bike to save time and is a fairly flat, wide roadbed with one notable washout-prone reroute near the start and a South Fork Sauk River crossing (log/footbridge) about a mile in. The road ends at the Monte Cristo ghost-town townsite (old mining buildings, informal camping). Pick up the signed Poodle Dog Pass/Twin Lakes trail behind the townsite and climb switchbacks about 1.5 miles and 1,600 ft to Poodle Dog Pass, passing Silver Lake. From the pass, continue on the Twin Lakes Trail — mostly well-graded but with occasional deadfall — to Twin Lakes (a popular basin for overnight scramblers), crossing granite slabs on the final approach; Sunday Creek, about 1.25 miles before the lakes, is the last reliable water source before the climb. From Twin Lakes (~5,000 ft), leave the trail and go cross-country up the east side/east crest of East Twin Peak, dropping into boulder fields around 5,300-5,800 ft, then trending up heather benches below cliff bands. Above roughly 6,300 ft the route works past a buttress via one of two class 3-4 options (a crack/chimney move on the left, or an easier move right into a ~50-ft gully) — this short section has minimal exposure but the gully above is steep with loose rock, so parties should stay close together and wear helmets. Above the gully, class 2-3 slabs and scree lead across the southwest face to the base of the summit block, finishing with a short class 3 corkscrew move around the final cliff band to the top. Route-finding through the boulder fields and buttress is the main crux of the approach; snow lingering into early summer on the upper ledges makes the route significantly more hazardous and it's best attempted after it has melted out.
approach_variant_names: Twin Lakes saddle and the west spur
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly — this is a downclimb/walk-off with no rappelling anywhere on the route (rappels: 0). From the summit block, reverse the class 3 corkscrew moves and downclimb the southwest-facing slabs and scree back to the buttress; reverse the class 3-4 crack/chimney (or the gully move used on the way up), taking care with loose rock in the gully — do not descend directly below other party members. Continue down through the heather benches and boulder fields back to Twin Lakes, then follow the Twin Lakes Trail over Poodle Dog Pass and down to Monte Cristo, and retrace the old mining road (or coast it on a bike) back to Barlow Pass. Parties note the descent typically goes noticeably faster than the ascent once the route-finding through the boulder fields/buttress is known (some parties report under 3 hours down vs. 4+ up). Main descent hazards are the same loose gully/buttress terrain as on the ascent and, in shoulder season, lingering snow on the ledge traverse below the summit.
current.detailed_rack: No roped gear is required for the standard ascent in good summer conditions - it's an off-trail alpine scramble. A short rope and a few slings are worth carrying as a security option for the class 4 chimney/crack move and the summit cliff-band bypass, though most parties climb the route unroped.
current.pro_needs: Essentially none for the standard summer scramble; any rope/slings carried are for optional security at the class 4 move and cliff band, not for sustained protection.
bivy: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
current.rope_note: Confirmed non-technical: no rope or rock climbing gear is needed to reach the summit — Class 3 scramble up the west spur with one 4th-class move gaining the SW face; exposure but no fixed pro used.

name: Complete South Buttress
beta: This route picks up the South Buttress ridge system far below the standard start, following easy, ledgy 3rd/4th-class slabs at the toe of the buttress for many pitches before the terrain steepens and merges with the standard South Buttress's wandering 5.6-5.8 climbing described in that route's beta. Two rappels of roughly half-rope length descend into gaps/notches along the lower ridge crest as part of the route (either ascending past or reversing them on descent), from fixed tat anchors that sources flag as dated.
overview: The Complete South Buttress extends the Regular South Buttress route by starting on a rock ridge lower down than the standard approach, adding enjoyable 3rd/4th class and easy 5th class climbing for a longer day of alpine travel before joining the standard South Buttress line.

current.approach: Follow the same approach as the standard South Buttress: from the long pullout on the north side of SR 20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, take the climbers' trail down through forest, across the creek (last reliable water — fill up here), and up into the meadows/boulder field below the peak, to roughly 6,500 ft. Instead of continuing to the standard South Buttress gully, leave the trail here and contour southeast (off-trail, on talus/heather benches) around to the southwest edge of the buttress, where the Complete South Buttress begins on easy, ledgy 3rd/4th-class slabs at the toe of the lower ridge — well below where the standard route ropes up. This adds meaningful distance and elevation gain over the standard approach since you're picking up the buttress much lower on the mountain; budget extra time versus the ~1.5-2 hour standard approach.
approach_variant_names: State Creek approach, continuing low to the buttress toe
current.descent: The lower ridge extension itself includes two rappels of roughly half-rope length into gaps/notches along the ridge crest, from fixed tat anchors — expect these to need backup or replacement webbing; the tat is dated. These are encountered as part of the route (either ascending past them or reversing them on the way down), not the final summit descent. Once you top out and join/finish on the standard South Buttress's upper terrain, the true summit descent follows the same two options as the South Buttress: the West Ridge (roughly 4 single-rope rappels from bolted chain anchors plus significant downclimbing and route-finding through old tat stations, generally the faster option — a 60m rope is reportedly just long enough, 70m gives margin) or reversing the full buttress with 12+ single-rope rappels on a mix of fixed and natural/gear anchors back down through the notch and gully system, plus the two half-rope tat rappels through the lower ridge's gaps/cols to fully retrace the Complete route back to the ~6,500 ft contour point. Either way, once back at the trail you retrace the standard approach down to the SR 20 pullout.
current.detailed_rack: Carry the same rack as the standard South Buttress -- a single rack 0.3-3 in with doubles 0.5-2 in, nuts, and an optional #4 for the summit offwidth -- plus a rope long enough for the two half-rope rappels on the lower-ridge extension. Fixed tat anchors exist at those rappels but may need inspection or backup webbing.
rack: Optional #4 cam for the summit offwidth
Rope long enough for two half-rope rappels on the lower-ridge extension
current.pro_needs: Same rack as the standard South Buttress; carry extra webbing/cord to back up the two aged tat rappel anchors on the lower-ridge extension.
bivy: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy, south side
current.rope_note: A trip report records a 70 m 9.2 mm rope. Long wandering line up slabs/overhangs/chimneys with the 5.8 crux (an offwidth) near the top before an easy final scramble. Approach involves a snow gully — ice axe/crampons useful early season.

name: Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer
beta: Begins on a wide granite apron with pleasant knobs and good crack protection low down; the crux 'Middle C' section (roughly pitches 7-10) climbs sustained 5.8 friction slab, including a runout quartz-dike pitch with small stair-step edges. Above, the route passes the 'Bubba Compactor' ledge and an 'Inverted Prow' dihedral before ridge-running to the top, with views over Buckeye Basin to Darrington.
overview: A long, 14-pitch alpine slab climb from a bivy bench up to the summit ridge, featuring sustained 5.8 friction on several pitches and a crusty ridge-running finish above Buckeye Basin.

current.approach: From Highway 530 in Darrington, go south on Madison Avenue to the T, turn right on Darrington Street and follow it as it becomes Squire Creek Road (FS 2040) to the washout that blocks it. Walk or bike the old roadbed past the landslide crossing to the Squire Creek Trail #654 sign, then continue 8–10 minutes to two cut logs on either side of the track, with old logging cable low and just right of it. A few steps past the logs, turn right on a well-beaten boot track down to Squire Creek and ford it where it is shallowest — hard in early season or after storms. Across the creek, follow a climbers' track right (downstream); it soon turns uphill, crosses a tributary (also hard early in the season), climbs through old-growth forest and drops left into two gullies, which it follows up. The top of the second gully is steep and dirty and opens onto a grassy saddle with good bivy sites, near the start of Concerto. Allow about 3 hours from the car. This turn-off comes before the one for Waterfall Basin, which is farther along at a wide streambed of white boulders.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
current.descent: Rappel the line of ascent on the route's fixed chain anchors; several rappels need a full 60 m rope. There is no walk-off, so plan the descent as rappels from the summit crest back to the grassy saddle.
current.detailed_rack: Standard single rack to 3 inches, supplemented by hand-drilled 3/8" stainless-steel wedge bolts with modern hangers on the friction sections; anchors are mostly fixed stainless chain (some tree anchors on the upper pitches).
current.pro_needs: A mix of gear placements in cracks low on the route and bolt protection through the sustained friction-slab crux pitches (7-10); the quartz-dike pitch is noted as runout between bolts.
bivy: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac

name: North Face
beta: This Grade II alpine rock climb starts at the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch and follows a clear crack system with minimal route-finding required. The route can be easily combined with Liberty Bell's Beckey Route as both start from the same approach gully. Moderate protection and gear-handling experience required.
overview: The original 1956 Beckey/Parrott line and Concord Tower's most popular route: a compact, three-pitch crack-and-corner climb up the north face on generally good granite to the small summit, often combined with Liberty Bell's Beckey Route via the shared notch.

current.approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20, about 0.5 mile past milepost 162 and about 1 mile west of Washington Pass. Follow the well-graded, well-maintained Blue Lake Trail through forest and past small tarns/streams for roughly 1.5-2 miles as it climbs into the open basin below the Liberty Bell group. Watch on your left (south/east side of the trail) for a signed, well-trodden climbers' path (Liberty Bell Trail #727) branching off shortly after the trail crosses a small stream near a meadow — this is easy to miss if you're not looking for it, and is the standard access to the Liberty Bell / Concord Tower massif rather than continuing on to Blue Lake itself. The climbers' path climbs steeply through slabs, talus, and heather meadow into upper 'Liberty Bowl,' gaining roughly 1,900-2,000 ft from the trailhead (figure 1.5-2.5 hours from the trailhead depending on fitness and snow conditions) to reach the gully/notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower (the Liberty Bell-Concord col, roughly 7,400 ft). This entry gully is frequently snow-filled and can stay icy into late June — many early-season parties carry an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) for it. Because the gully's rock is held together by snow much of the season, rockfall risk rises noticeably once the snow melts out, so helmet up before entering it and be mindful of parties above/below. The North Face route begins essentially at the top of this notch.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
Early-season snow to the notch
current.descent: Descend by rappelling back down the North Face line itself — do not try to walk off. From the summit, move to the double-bolt rap chains (a short, slightly awkward step/slither over the summit block gets you to the anchor) and make three single-rope rappels with a 60m rope: rappel 1 goes from the summit chains down the upper face; rappel 2 starts from a bolted anchor just below Pitch 3's 5.0 slab section and drops to the bushy, tree-dotted ledge atop Pitch 1; rappel 3 goes from that ledge back to the base of the climb at the notch. The first two stations are fixed bolts/chains; the last, on the pitch-1 ledge, is a tree or bush, so carry webbing and a rap ring. From the base, reverse the approach: descend the gully/climbers' path back through Liberty Bowl to the Blue Lake Trail and out to the trailhead. Note this is distinct from the South Face descent option some parties use when linking Concord with Lexington Tower — that alternate line is only 2 rappels but the first is a full 30m pull requiring the rope's middle mark to be set correctly at the anchor; the direct North Face descent described here is the standard 3-rappel version.
current.detailed_rack: A light single alpine rack with stoppers and cams to 2-3 inches plus slings is sufficient for the short pitches.
current.pro_needs: Modest natural pro on moderate granite.

name: South Route
beta: Copper Peak is most often climbed out of a Copper Basin camp above Holden Village, frequently paired with neighboring Mount Fernow (the two are connected by a rugged, 'contrived' ridge traverse with significant elevation loss/regain that is not generally recommended as a link-up). The route is a long, remote approach — boat, shuttle, and trail — followed by moderate but exposed scrambling rather than sustained technical climbing; the crux is routefinding among several ridge notches and a short 4th-class step near the top. A Mountaineers trip report combining Copper Peak and Mount Fernow in one outing logged roughly 9.7 miles round trip and just under 6,000 ft of cumulative gain by GPS, though that figure spans both summits, not Copper Peak alone, so it is not used here as a route-specific stat.
overview: Copper Peak (8,965 ft) is the second-highest summit in the Entiat Mountains and Washington's 21st-highest peak (19th on the 'Bulger' list), rising just 0.88 mile north of Mount Fernow in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. Unlike Fernow and Seven Fingered Jack, Copper Peak's slopes drain north into Railroad Creek toward Lake Chelan, and the standard route reflects that: climbers reach it from Holden Village by boat-and-shuttle (or a long cross-country alternative over Spider Gap), not from the Entiat River road system. First climbed in August 1937 by Franklin Bennet, Edgar Courtwright, and Toivo Hagman, it is one of the least-visited Bulgers, with real routefinding, a short glacier/snowfield crossing, and an exposed class 4 ridge finish above a long, remote approach.

current.approach: Copper Peak has no drivable trailhead — access is via the Lake Chelan ferry from Fields Point/Chelan to Lucerne Landing, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up to Holden Village (~3,300 ft) in the Railroad Creek valley, Glacier Peak Wilderness. From the village, follow the old mine road/Railroad Creek Trail east roughly 0.5 mile and cross Railroad Creek (footbridge or ford, depending on season) to reach a large tailings pile at about 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off. This climbers'/boot trail climbs steeply for about 0.7 mile up a hillside (partly burned) before entering the Copper Creek drainage, then parallels the creek south for roughly 3 miles, gaining to about 5,600 ft where it crosses a flat, open bench — this is the standard base camp (Copper Basin) used by nearly all parties. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft, but a continuing boot path pushes on toward the Copper–Entiat Divide near 7,200 ft. From camp, leave the trail, ford Copper Creek to its west side, and traverse/ascend talus and slabs alongside the outlet stream draining the Southeast Glacier remnant on the peak's east face. Reliable water is available along Railroad and Copper Creeks and near camp, but carry what you need above the basin. Hazards include two creek crossings that run higher and faster during early-season snowmelt, a steep and unmaintained burned-hillside section just above the valley floor, loose Class 3 talus/scree approaching the glacier, and real crevasse hazard on the (much-diminished but still present) Southeast Glacier — rope up for glacier travel, especially early in the season. Above the glacier a loose Class 3 gully gains a notch on the ridge's north side; a steep snowfield/snow gully beyond can require crampons and, if icy, a belay. The high camp near 6,500 ft has running water beside it and flat room for about one two-person tent (late August).
approach_variant_names: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
Phelps Creek over Spider Gap
current.descent: Nearly all parties reverse the ascent line (Southeast Glacier / upper Northeast Ridge route) rather than finding a separate walk-off: downclimb the Class 3 ridge (one short, more exposed Class 3+/4 move is commonly reported near the summit ridge, and some parties carry a short hand line for one airy notch — this is a fixed handline, not a rappel) back to the north-side notch, downclimb (or belay, if icy) the steep snowfield/gully back onto the Southeast Glacier remnant, cross the glacier roped and mindful of crevasses, descend the loose Class 3 gully back into the upper basin, then retrace the boot path and Copper Creek Trail to Holden Village. Multiple trip reports for this route explicitly describe downclimbing the ascent line — one notes glissading available snow where possible — and none report rappelling; this is a downclimb/walk-off route, not a rappel descent.
current.detailed_rack: Most parties climb this unroped; no rack is placed. A light rack (a few slings, a 30m rope) is worth having for the short, exposed class 4 moves near the summit notches, where some parties prefer to belay rather than solo them.
rack: 30m rope for the crossing and an optional belay
A few slings + small cams/nuts for the exposed class 4 step (optional)
current.pro_needs: A light rack (a few slings and small cams/nuts) covers the short exposed class 4 step; most parties otherwise scramble the class 3 sections unroped in good conditions and only rope up for the glacier/snowfield crossing.
current.rope_note: Rope up for the glacier. The Southeast Glacier remnant is small and its crevasses are usually minor, but crossing it is the one place on this route where the rope is not optional, so carry a harness and a 30 m rope alongside the ice axe and crampons. Above it most parties scramble the Class 3 ground unroped, but there is a short, exposed and insecure Class 4 step near the summit ridge: a few slings and a small cam or nut let you belay that rather than solo it, and some parties carry a short hand line for one airy notch. Keep the rope out on the way down - the steep snowfield below the notch is worth a belay if it has gone hard, and the glacier is crossed roped again on the way out.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Cosho Peak (aka 'Ragged End') is the westernmost of four consecutive 8,000+ ft summits on Ragged Ridge along with Mesahchie, Katsuk, and Kimtah, and is typically the farthest point climbers reach via the Easy Pass approach. No technical rock climbing or serious glacier travel is strictly required for the standard route, but the terrain is very rough: miles of talus, sidehill traversing, and gully scrambling connect Easy Pass to the peak. Most parties combine Cosho with neighboring Kimtah Peak, descending Kimtah's south gully to the connecting saddle before making the final push up Cosho.
overview: Cosho Peak (8,332 ft), nicknamed "Ragged End," is the westernmost and lowest of the four standard Ragged Ridge Bulger scrambles (Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah, Cosho), sitting above the Kimtah Glacier on its northeast flank deep in North Cascades National Park. The name comes from Chinook Jargon "cosho" ("hog"). No technical climbing is required on the standard route — it's mostly loose talus, some snow, and about 200-250 ft of 3rd-class rock on the upper east face — but the very long, remote approach makes it one of the least-visited Bulgers; it's typically climbed once as a checklist peak, almost always paired with neighboring Kimtah.

current.approach: Start at the Easy Pass Trailhead on the south side of SR 20 (Easy Pass Trail, North Cascades National Park, backcountry permit required for camping). The trail climbs steadily through forest, crossing Easy Pass Creek three times, and breaks out into subalpine meadows and heather benches before the final push to Easy Pass at about 6,550 ft — roughly 3.5-3.6 miles and 2,700-2,800 ft of gain, typically 2-3 hours. Steep snow can linger on this stretch well into July, and an ice axe is recommended; the tread can be hard to follow across snowfields, and the meadows are fragile, so stay on trail/rock where possible. From the pass, leave the high traverse and descend the Fisher Creek side: the trail switchbacks roughly 30 times, losing nearly 1,400 ft, into the Fisher Creek valley. Follow the Fisher Creek Trail west/downstream along the north side of the creek for about 3 miles (the creek itself is a reliable water source) to Cosho Camp (~3,900-4,200 ft, creekside, a designated NPS camping zone and the logical base camp for this peak). From Cosho Camp continue west on the trail roughly another mile until due south of the Cosho/Kimtah saddle, then leave the trail and begin climbing one of the gullies leading north, starting around 3,800 ft. This off-trail leg is the crux of the approach: steep talus, grass, and some solid rock for about 4,000 ft of gain to a saddle at roughly 7,830 ft, with sustained bushwhacking through trees and brush in the first thousand feet and loose, tedious scree higher up. Alternatively, some parties camp higher, in a basin south of Mesahchie Peak (~6,600 ft) reached by traversing south of the Easy Pass ridge at 6,600-6,700 ft across numerous small gullies and buttresses (~1 mile, ~5 hours from the trailhead), then climb about 800 ft to a 7,400 ft bench and traverse west to the Cosho/Kimtah col — a shorter final push at the cost of a longer, more exposed high traverse to reach camp. Expect this to be a full, long trekking day regardless of which camp is used; this is a remote, seldom-visited corner of the park and route-finding care is needed in poor visibility.
approach_variant_names: Cosho Camp to the 7,830 ft saddle and the north snowfield
From Kimtah, down the south gully and the connecting traverse
current.descent: This is a scramble, not a technical rock route, and no rappels are used — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-4 upper section back to the saddle (accounts vary on the exact character here: some parties describe a short, fun class 2-3 scramble from a notch just below the true summit; others describe roughly 250 vertical feet of class 3-4 terrain near the top, including an airy, exposed 4th-class ledge system that requires careful downclimbing, 250-300 ft, back toward the col). From the ~7,830 ft saddle, downclimb the steep talus/grass/brush gully back to about 3,800 ft where you rejoin the Fisher Creek Trail, then retrace the approach: east on the Fisher Creek Trail past Cosho Camp, back up the ~1,400 ft of switchbacks to Easy Pass, and down the Easy Pass Trail to the trailhead. Loose rock and scree on the gully descent are the main hazard — care is needed not to kick rock onto party members below — and lingering snow in the upper gullies/saddle area into midsummer may warrant an ice axe and caution on the downclimb. No rappel gear is required for this route under normal summer conditions.
current.detailed_rack: The standard route is an unroped scramble for experienced parties in good conditions, so no traditional rack is used. Some parties carry a rope and a light rack/slings for the final rock step or for crevasse rescue on glaciated variants, though it is not required for the standard south-side ridge route in typical late-summer conditions.
current.pro_needs: Typically scrambled unroped on 3rd-class rock; a rope/light rack is rarely carried but can help on the exposed 4th-class Kimtah–Cosho connecting ridge if linking the two peaks.
current.rope_note: Ragged Ridge peak; final approach is moderate snow (ice axe useful) then ~200ft of solid 3rd-class rock to the summit — no rope used in trip reports found.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: From the West Fork Buttermilk Trailhead, follow maintained Trail #411 through forest, across several fords, and around a large washout to Fish Creek Pass (7,480 ft). Leave the trail there and climb the open southeast ridge directly to the summit on a boot path that becomes class 2 boulders in the last few hundred feet — about 0.4 mile and 900 ft of gain from the pass.
overview: Courtney Peak (8,394 ft) is a Class 2-3 scramble on Sawtooth Ridge in the Methow Mountains, within the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. Its parent peak is Star Peak (8,690 ft), 0.83 mi to the southeast; Courtney is widely regarded among Washington scramblers as having one of the best summit panoramas in the wilderness, taking in Star and Oval Peaks, the Oval Lakes basin, and distant glaciated North Cascades summits. The peak was officially named in 1985 for Ray Courtney (1920-1982), a longtime Stehekin packer who died leading a horse pack trip in the area. It's commonly climbed together with Oval and Star Peaks from a single high camp at Star Lake, and is a popular early-October target for larch color along the crest.

current.approach: From the West Fork Buttermilk Trailhead (elev. ~3,960 ft, at the end of FR-4300-500 off East Buttermilk Creek Road/FR-43, reached via Twisp River Road west of Twisp), follow the West Fork Buttermilk Trail #411 into the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. The trail climbs steadily up the West Fork of Buttermilk Creek through ponderosa pine and larch forest. Expect several unbridged crossings of the creek and its side drainages that can run high and fast with snowmelt through June — plan on wet feet or careful boulder-hopping in early season. Maintenance is light and blowdowns are common in the lower miles in recent years; a GPS track is worth carrying since flagging/tread can thin out where deadfall forces detours around downed timber. At roughly 7–7.5 miles and about 3,500 ft of cumulative gain, the trail tops out at Fish Creek Pass (~7,480 ft), a major junction where it meets the Fish Creek Trail #1248; Star Lake sits just below/north of the pass and is the last reliable water source before the summit push, and a common camp for parties splitting the trip over two days. From the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up the obvious boot path/climbers' trail that switchbacks northwest up the open ridge toward Courtney Peak. This use trail gains roughly 900–1,000 ft on easy class 2 tundra and talus with a good game/climbers' path most of the way; a few hundred feet below the summit it steepens into larger class 2+ boulders that require careful hopping and some route-finding to the summit block. Snow can linger in the gullies near the pass and on the upper ridge into July, so an ice axe is worth carrying for early-season (June) attempts. Round trip from trailhead to summit and back runs about 17 miles with roughly 4,700 ft of total gain — this matches a long car-to-car day or an overnight with camp at Star Lake, not the longer Star/Oval combined traverse some parties do as a multi-summit epic. Past the washout roughly three miles in, fallen trees still need to be climbed over in early October, and the creek is crossed on a log; flagging marks the easiest line through the washout.
approach_variant_names: West Fork Buttermilk Trail #411 to Fish Creek Pass
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly: downclimb the class 2+ boulder field below the summit back onto the boot path, then follow the use trail down the southeast ridge to Fish Creek Pass. From the pass, rejoin the West Fork Buttermilk Trail #411 for the full hike back down to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb the entire way — there is no rappelling on the standard route, and most parties do not carry a rope. The main descent hazards are the loose class 2+ talus just below the summit (careful foot placement, stay alert for rockfall onto parties below) and, near the pass and on the upper ridge, lingering snow or wet scree that can be slick into early summer — an ice axe/microspikes are useful insurance in June. Some parties link Courtney with Star Peak and/or Oval Peak and descend via a different drainage (e.g., toward Eagle Creek) as part of a car-shuttle loop, but that requires a second vehicle staged at a different trailhead and is a variation on, not the standard version of, this out-and-back route.
current.detailed_rack: None — this is an unroped Class 2 (occasional easy Class 3) scramble; no rack is carried.
current.pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
current.rope_note: Straightforward Class 2-3 climb up the SE ridge from Fish Creek Pass to a wide summit; a simple, non-technical scramble.

name: Standard Route (Southeast Ridge via Jackita Ridge / Crater Lake Trail)
beta: Widely regarded as a fun, non-technical but sustained 3rd-class scramble; the crux is a short, loose, exposed gully section below the true summit that is marked with painted yellow X's/arrows and requires careful route-finding among several cliff bands. Most parties do it as one very long day (~15 miles RT) or split it with a camp at Crater Lake.
overview: A long approach-heavy trail hike from the Canyon Creek Trailhead up Jackita Ridge Trail to Crater Lake basin, then an off-trail southeast-ridge scramble past a false summit to a loose, exposed 3rd-class gully near 7,600 ft that is marked with fading yellow paint and cairns, finishing on scree/talus to the summit plateau and old lookout site.

current.approach: From the Canyon Creek Trailhead (1,900 ft) on SR 20 (32.8 mi east of Marblemount / 55.1 mi west of Winthrop), take Jackita Ridge Trail #738, crossing Granite Creek on a bridge and fording Canyon Creek near the start. The trail climbs steeply through timber via numerous switchbacks (roughly 55) gaining about 3,400 ft over 4 miles to a junction near 5,000-5,260 ft, with views opening onto Crater and Jack Mountains above timberline. Turn left onto the Crater Lake Trail (brushy, user-maintained) for about a mile to Crater Lake (about 5,800 ft) below the peak's south side.
approach_variant_names: Canyon Creek trailhead, Jackita Ridge #738 and the Crater Lake trail #746
Devils Dome loop from the East Bank trailhead
current.descent: From the summit, descend the scree/talus slopes back to the top of the crux gully and downclimb it carefully, following the same painted yellow X's/arrows and cairns used on the ascent (parties note this section is loose and exposure-sensitive both ways). Continue around the false summit's west side back onto the southeast ridge, drop into Crater Lake basin, and rejoin Jackita Ridge Trail for the descent to the Canyon Creek Trailhead, re-fording Canyon Creek.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is used on the standard route; it is climbed as an unroped scramble. Some parties carry a light rope for the crux gully as a personal safety margin, particularly for less-experienced scramblers or in wet conditions.
current.pro_needs: None required for the standard line; it is not a protected/roped route. An ice axe may be prudent in early season if snow lingers in the gully or on the upper slopes.

name: Crescendo of the Sarcophagus Breathing
beta: Single pitch sport climb featuring increasingly overhanging jugs leading to a crux mantle move. After a no-hands rest ledge, a second mini crux around 5.10c difficulty, followed by easier slab climbing to anchor on a large ledge. Route passes through some orange-streaked rock.
overview: 5.11b sport route on Keechelus Ridge's East Face near Snoqualmie Pass, featuring powerful jug climbing, a crux mantle, and spectacular position.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive east on I-90 to Snoqualmie Pass and take Exit 54, crossing to the north side of the freeway before turning onto FR 4832, then following it onto FR 4934 to the small trailhead pullout. On foot, cross the road and hike up a spur road for about 15 minutes to a flat bench, then pick up a cairned trail heading north into the forest to a rocky area, staying on the main climber's trail through a short, steeper forest section to reach the crag — roughly 25-30 minutes total from the car. A Northwest Forest Pass is generally expected for parking at national forest trailheads in this corridor.
current.descent: Single lower from the top chain anchor; at 75 ft the route is well within range of a 60m rope.
current.detailed_rack: 10 bolts with chain anchor
current.pro_needs: Sport climbing route with full bolt protection.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route, 75 ft (23m), 10 bolts, chain anchor. Overhanging jugs to a crux mantle, rest ledge, second ~5.10c mini-crux, then easier slab to anchor.

name: South Route
beta: This classic Beckey-era first ascent combines a roughly 46-50 mile round-trip backpacking approach with technical alpine climbing. The route is accessed via the Hannegan Trailhead system, passing through the Chilliwack River drainage to Whatcom Pass, then crossing Whatcom Glacier and the heavily crevassed Crooked Thumb Glacier to reach the moraine basecamp. The summit push ascends the obvious northwest couloir with simul-climbing on 40-45 degree snow using snow flukes for protection, transitioning to Class 4-5 scrambling and exposed ledges on the narrow snow-and-rock gully accessing the north ridge. The route requires strong alpine climbing and scrambling skills, efficient rope management, and excellent route-finding in complex terrain.
overview: A rarely repeated snow-and-rock line to Crooked Thumb's narrow granite summit fin. From the snow saddle just north of the peak, climb the obvious northwest couloir to the north ridge, cross loose, scree-covered ledges onto the west face, and climb a vertical crack in the west-face headwall, which is the crux, then finish up the south ridge to the summit. Route-finding on the headwall is the main difficulty.

current.approach: Start at Hannegan Trailhead (3,100 ft) at the end of Ruth Creek Road (FR 32). Take the Hannegan Pass Trail roughly 4 miles and ~2,500 ft of gain up through subalpine forest and meadow to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft). From the pass, drop off the north side on the Chilliwack River Trail into the Chilliwack River valley — this loses most of the elevation just gained and is the start of a long valley traverse. The trail passes Copper Creek Camp (~9 mi) and U.S. Cabin Camp (~12 mi); expect brushy tread near U.S. Cabin Camp and, in blowdown years, stretches of downed timber (one trip report logged roughly two hours to move 1.5 miles through fallen trunks and limbs beyond the cable-car crossing). Cross the Chilliwack River on the hand-pulled cable car (a mandatory, somewhat exposed crossing — the river is not reliably fordable). Beyond the crossing, pick up the Brush Creek Trail, which climbs steadily (generally in better condition, with only scattered blowdown) to Whatcom Pass (5,206 ft, ~17 mi in). From Whatcom Camp near the pass, leave maintained trail and traverse cross-country below Whatcom Peak's northeast flank via the Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass (about 4.5 hours and 1,750 ft of gain from Whatcom Camp); Perfect Pass has reliable running water and is a common high camp. From Perfect Pass, rope up for glacier travel and ascend the Challenger Glacier to a high bench around 8,100 ft, then descend through the West Challenger Notch onto the Crooked Thumb Glacier, where a lateral-moraine camp serves as the base for the climb. This is a serious multi-day glaciated approach (round trip on the order of 40+ miles): carry a rope, crevasse-rescue gear, and an ice axe/crampons for the Whatcom and Challenger Glacier crossings, and treat the cable-car crossing and brush/blowdown sections of the Chilliwack River Trail as the main non-glacier hazards. The Crooked Thumb Glacier itself can be severely crevassed with moats late in the season.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier and through West Challenger Notch
Big Beaver valley and Wiley Ridge
current.descent: Reverse the climbing route from the summit rather than continuing over the north ridge. Down-climb the loose, exposed class 4-5 summit ridge and ledges just south of the true summit using running belays and gear placements — this terrain is horribly loose, so treat every hold as suspect and keep the rope short between placements. At the top of the crux headwall, make one single-strand rappel down the ~10-ft near-vertical crack (roughly 5.8+ or 5.2/A1); a single 30-40m rope reaches the ledge below. Continue down and along the loose class 4-5 ledges around the north ridge's pinnacles to a rock horn draped with old rappel slings (do not trust weathered fixed tat — back it up with your own cord); from this horn, make two rappels on doubled ropes (the one party to record this descent joined a 40m and a 30m 6.9mm alpine rope) to reach an exit ledge above the couloir — a single 60m rope doubled, or two 30m ropes, works as a substitute. From the exit ledge, down-climb the 40-45° northwest snow couloir, placing snow pickets or flukes as protection if conditions are firm or icy, back to the saddle just north of the peak and down to camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. From camp, reverse the full glaciated approach (Challenger Glacier, West Challenger Notch, Perfect Pass, Whatcom Glacier traverse, Whatcom Pass, Brush Creek Trail, Chilliwack River Trail and cable car, Hannegan Pass) back to the Hannegan Trailhead. All anchors encountered are natural/fixed-sling (horn or gear) — there is no bolted rappel line on this route. Total rappel count on the one recorded descent: 3 (one at the headwall crack, two from the north-ridge horn) — a long rappel and a short one from the horn, not a matched pair. This is not fixed: a soloist who found a low-angle, barely-fifth-class wall on the southeast side bypassing the summit cliffs downclimbed the whole route with no rappels at all, and a traverse party crossed the peak without a rope.
current.detailed_rack: For rock protection: bring a half rack of cams (0.5-3 size range) and a selection of nuts for the Class 4-5 rock pitches; supplementary trad gear (slings, tat, quickdraws) for anchoring and protection. Snow protection: minimum 6 snow flukes or pickets for running belays and rappel anchors on steep snow couloirs. Rappel/belay: 2 ropes (40m + 30m, 6-7mm), two carabiners per climber, locking carabiners for anchors, and autoblock backup devices. The rock grades (up to 5.8 in sections) and sustained 40-45 degree snow require serious alpine climbing competency and efficient rope management.
current.pro_needs: Team should bring 2 ropes for efficient rappelling and running belay systems. Six to eight snow flukes/pickets are minimum for the sustained snow couloir section. Redundant rappel anchors essential due to exposure and loose rock. Slings and quickdraws for linking natural anchors (rock and snow features). Prussiks or autoblock systems for rappel backups on steep terrain.
bivy: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp
current.rope_note: Two thin ropes, roughly 30 m and 40 m, joined for the rappels off the north-ridge horn; a single 60 m rope doubled, or two 30 m ropes, substitutes. The headwall rappel is made on a single strand.

name: The Swarm
