beta: Eight pitches of varied climbing culminate in four headwall pitches rated 5.10-5.11, protected by natural gear from bolted anchors (anchors placed on lead for everything above 5.9; the route's only protection bolt is on pitch 6), with natural gear protecting the lower and upper pitches. Notable pitches include "The Gem" (a splitter finger crack, pitch 3) and a sustained dihedral-jamming crux pitch (pitch 6).
overview: A modern, sustained 5.11 alpine testpiece up Cutthroat's East Face, with four gear-protected headwall pitches (5.10-5.11) on bolted anchors linking natural, less-traveled terrain below and above — a quality alternative to the crowded Liberty Bell group just to the south.

current.approach: Begin as for the North Ridge (via the South Buttress approach trail or the Rainy Pass/PCT option), then continue toward the East Face, avoiding steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall.
current.descent: Rappel the route (the four bolted headwall pitches allow a two-rope rappel), or descend via the South Buttress, switching to the West Ridge if other parties are on the buttress.
current.detailed_rack: Double rack through #3, single #4; offset cams (.1-.75) helpful but optional; 10-12 alpine draws and one triple-length draw for pitch 3.
current.pro_needs: Bolted anchors on the four main headwall pitches; natural gear (cams/nuts) protects the lower approach pitches and the upper exit pitches.

name: West Ridge
beta: Grade II, 5th-class climbing to about 5.6 (harder direct variations reach 5.7). Short approach from highway. Rock improves significantly higher on ridge. Fair granite in approach, improves on ridge. Moderate exposure. Quick alpine climb from a pullout on SR 20 west of Washington Pass. Uncrowded route.
overview: The West Ridge is the easiest technical line up Cutthroat Peak, a short scrambly route with a few low-fifth-class steps that makes a quicker alternative to the long South Buttress.

current.approach:
Park on the broad shoulder of SR-20 roughly half a mile west of the Blue Lake trailhead, where there is a view through the trees to the peak; parties often meet at the Blue Lake lot and drive the short distance west to it. Head up from there into the basin below the peak.

Coming up into the basin, stay somewhat left to arrive at the notch at the base of the west ridge. That notch, rather than the ridge crest above it, is the reference point — from it, traverse ledges for about a hundred feet to the foot of a shallow gully running up and left onto the ridge.
approach_variant_names: Roadside pullout west of the Blue Lake Trailhead
current.descent: Most parties reverse the ridge with short downclimbs and rappels from bolted anchors, the first just west of the summit, and rappel into the southwest gully at the foot of the ridge. Below the gully, drop skier's right onto a sandy rib with a faint climbers' track, then into another gully farther skier's right for the lower part; going straight down leads into loose ground. Pick up the climbers' path through the State Creek brush back to the highway.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack with stoppers and cams to 2 inches plus slings covers the short technical steps; many parties simul or pitch out only the steeper bits.
current.pro_needs: Minimal pro; mostly scrambling with a few short roped steps.
bivy: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby

name: Czech it Out
beta: Crimpy, slightly overhanging start leads to great holds and a nice outlook; 7 bolts to two anchor stations.
overview: Route on Megadike South mentioned in area descriptions.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike South: drive 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and park on either side of the road just before the bridge over the river. Scramble up the steep hillside on the NW side of the road above the bridge abutment, then continue uphill along the dike to a passable gully.
current.descent: Lower from either of the two anchor stations on a single strand.
current.detailed_rack: 7 bolts to two anchor stations.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted (7 bolts).
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Megadike South (The Dikes, WA). 70m recommended given crag-wide walls up to 120-140ft.

name: Dark Glacier Route
beta: Dark Peak is regarded as an adventure/remoteness objective more than a technically hard one. After a boat-and-shuttle approach into the roadless Stehekin Valley, parties hike the Agnes Creek Trail (PCT) to a high camp, then leave the trail for a long, routefinding-heavy cross-country push -- either up the historically brushy, officially abandoned Swamp Creek climbers' path, or via a newer variant farther south on the PCT to Hemlock Camp -- gaining a basin below "Dark Fin Col." From the col, parties rope up, descend a loose slope onto the crevassed Dark Glacier, pick a line across it (the right side of the glacier is reported as a good line), and finish with a belayed crossing of the summit moat/bergschrund onto the rock ridge leading to the top. Reported early-to-mid-summer conditions give firm, well-bridged snow with minimal crevasse danger; by late summer more crevasses are exposed and the glacier becomes less stable.
overview: The standard route climbs Dark Peak's north-side Dark Glacier from a remote upper basin above Swamp Creek, then crosses a bergschrund/moat onto the summit rock ridge for a short scramble to the top -- a moderate glacier climb whose real difficulty is the long, brushy, multi-day approach rather than the technical climbing.

current.approach: Access begins in Chelan via the Lady of the Lake passenger ferry (Lady Express ~2.5 hrs or Lady II ~4 hrs) or floatplane to the roadless village of Stehekin, then a scheduled valley shuttle bus/van up the Stehekin Valley Road to High Bridge (~1,700 ft), the trailhead for the Agnes Creek Trail/PCT and the end of the road. From High Bridge there are two documented approach options to the base of the peak: (1) Traditional Swamp Creek approach -- hike the Agnes Creek Trail (PCT) south about 5-5.5 miles to Fivemile Camp (2,200 ft), continuing about 3 more miles (roughly 8-9 miles total from High Bridge) to Swamp Creek Camp (2,800 ft); leave the maintained trail and follow the long-unmaintained, heavily brushed Swamp Creek climbers' path upvalley, crossing Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and pushing through roughly a quarter mile of thick slide alder and vine maple, to reach a lower basin (often not until after dark for many parties); continue cross-country from the lower basin to the upper basin (about 4-5 hours of further travel, reaching roughly 4,300 ft), then kick steps up around 3,000 ft of steep, often snow-covered terrain (no established track) to the saddle/col below the glacier. (2) Newer PCT/Hemlock Camp variant -- continue farther south on the PCT roughly 12.5 miles from High Bridge to Hemlock Camp, then leave the trail and climb northwest through open forest and slopes (about 3,500 ft of gain) directly to Dark Fin Col, avoiding most of the Swamp Creek brush; this is reported as a substantially easier approach even though it is not the route most published descriptions still describe as standard. In early May the Agnes Creek section of the PCT was cleared by trail crews only as far as 1-2 miles short of Swamp Creek camp, after which about 30 trees lay across the tread; the camp itself was snow free that month in a low-snow year.
approach_variant_names: Swamp Creek climbers' path to the col
Crest trail to Hemlock Camp and the northwest climb
current.descent: There is no separate descent route documented -- parties down-climb the same line they climbed. From the summit, reverse the short scramble to the moat, get a belay or careful downclimb across the bergschrund/moat back onto glacier ice, and descend the Dark Glacier roped as a team, staying alert for crevasses that may be less obvious on the way down and for wet, loose rock along the glacier's rock margins. Regain Dark Fin Col, then descend the approach terrain (loose/steep slopes into the basin, and either the Swamp Creek brush or the PCT/Hemlock Camp slopes) back to high camp. Given how long and strenuous the round trip from camp is, most parties plan to be back at camp well before dark and treat the final hike out to High Bridge as a separate day to make the fixed ferry/shuttle departure.
current.detailed_rack: A standard glacier-travel rack rather than a rock rack: one rope per rope team, and 2-3 pickets and/or ice screws for crevasse-rescue anchors and to belay the short summit moat crossing. A basic crevasse-rescue kit (prusik cords or mechanical ascenders, a pulley, extra slings and locking carabiners) should be carried by each rope team. Little to no traditional rock protection is used on the standard line; the final scrambling is generally unroped in good conditions.
current.pro_needs: Protection needs on this route are glacier-travel oriented rather than rock-gear oriented: pickets or ice screws for crevasse-rescue anchors and a body or picket belay for the short, exposed moat/bergschrund crossing onto the summit ridge are the main technical protection used; the summit scramble itself is typically climbed unroped.
bivy: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain

name: Northeast Face Couloir
beta: From a bivouac at about 4,000 ft at the foot of the glacier, climb the glacier to the bergschrund and simul-climb the compact lower rock band (mid-fifth class in summer, hard to protect) to the right side of the large snowfield. Traverse left across the snowfield to the couloir, belay the crux pitches over iced slabs and a steep chockstone, and continue up the long, exposed upper couloir to the cornices where it meets the summit ridge at about 6,700 ft. The summit is a short way along the ridge.
overview: The Northeast Face Couloir climbs Davis Peak's huge northeast wall above Stetattle Creek, one of the biggest faces in the North Cascades: a compact lower rock band, a traverse left across a large snowfield, belayed crux pitches over iced slabs and a steep chockstone, then a long, exposed upper couloir to the cornices where it meets the summit ridge near 6,700 ft. It goes in summer as a rock-and-snow route and has been climbed in winter; the descent is the long south side.

current.approach: From Diablo, take the Stetattle Creek trail about 2 mi, drop about 200 ft to ford the creek opposite Davis Peak, then bushwhack and scramble a Class 3-4 rib, roping up for slabby sections, through slide alder above the cliffs to flat ground at the toe of the glacier, about 4,000 ft. Expect roughly eight or nine hours from the road. The whole Stetattle Creek Trail has been closed until further notice for post-fire hazards (falling dead trees and unstable ground); check its status with North Cascades National Park before a trip.
current.descent:
The northeast face has no easy retreat; descend the south side, which is long and unpleasant but walkable.

From the top of the couloir at about 6,700 ft, rappel from pitons onto the SE ridge (or continue up the ridge to the 7,054 ft summit first if time allows). Descend the south side following the South Slope and Ridge route in reverse: down the ridge crest, past the 5,720+ ft saddle, over or around Point 5872, and then straight down the sustained trackless forest of the south slope to the highway.

Daylight is the key. Descending the upper 1,500 ft in the light avoids the cliff bands, and the rappels off trees that come with getting them wrong. The forest below is thick, but the right line has no cliffs and little slide alder; allow about four hours from the top of the timber to the road. The timber is dense enough to hide landmarks, so navigate by compass to avoid ending up in Stetattle Creek.

You finish at the Gorge Creek bridge, about four highway miles from the parking in Diablo, so arrange a shuttle car.
current.detailed_rack: Rack used on the 2005 ascent: a full set of wires, knifeblades, lost arrows, and Friends/cams from #1 to #3.5, plus a picket would have been useful. Add a few short and medium ice screws — stubbies specifically, since the useful placements were in thin ice under an overhang and in the ice above the chockstone — and a single rope. The pitons are not optional: the rock is compact and the knifeblades proved their worth on the runout bulge below the chockstone. Belays were improvised from a cam, a stubby screw and a doubtful horn. Bring slings and tat for rappel anchors you may have to leave behind.
current.pro_needs: Poor to marginal throughout. The lower band is compact gneiss and was simul-climbed with long gaps between pieces; the crux traverse across a partially iced slab is terrain where a leader cannot afford to fall. Pins are the primary protection. The one properly protected move on the route is the chockstone itself — a cam below the roof and a stubby screw in the good ice on the left. On the upper couloir and rib, expect simul-climbing with occasional gear and very large exposure. Nothing about this route rewards a cam-only rack.

name: South Slope and Ridge
beta:
Almost all the difficulty here is brush, steepness and route-finding rather than climbing. The rock is rated Class 4, but that grade comes from a January ascent, when good snow may have covered the harder steps; the bare-rock difficulty and the number of pitches, if any, are not known.

From the Gorge Creek bridge at 1,096 ft the slope is sustained from the first step, gaining roughly 1,800 ft in the first half mile through small evergreens with a salal and brush understory. There is no trail, and numerous rock outcrops make navigation important. One recorded line: from near the highway curve, hike due north to about 2,800 ft, turn northeast and ascend to the 4,920+ ft point, then go straight uphill on a bearing of about 340 degrees true to Point 5872, where the south ridge becomes obvious. A party approaching via Gorge Creek instead took the South Buttress, turning cliff bands at about 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft on the right, moving through open timber and alpine snowfields, and reaching the South Davis saddle at 5,700 ft in 4.4 hours from the car; they described Class 2-3 scrambling on the buttress with slime-coated rock slabs near the top. A third account has the granite slabs starting around 4,850 ft after a brushy gully at 3,600 ft, bypassing Point 5872 to the north, and reaching a south-ridge viewpoint at 6,300 ft.

From the 5,720+ ft saddle, climb 200 ft of slab to the sharp ridge that leads to the summit. In good snow this is step-kicking; bare it is class 4 slab. In snow this is where the route's steepest ground is — the notch on the old standard south ridge line is reported at 65 degrees, which is precisely why skiers pushed a variation onto the southwest face. Above it the crest broadens into an almost level, wide-open ridge to the summit, one of the great walkable viewpoints in the range and simultaneously the top of the largest cornices most people will ever stand near. In summer that broad snow crest may instead be a scramble among rocks with steep drops on both sides.

There is also a variation that its climber did not rate: from the saddle, drop east into the basin under the east side of the south ridge, traverse up and north as far as possible, then turn west and climb beside the cliff edge. The turn involves a ten-foot step that looked trivial and was not — iced-in cracks and wrong-feeling holds, passed with ice-axe belays. The direct ridge, descended on the return, offered every ledge needed to get down. Take the ridge.

The southwest face is now the more popular finish, especially on snow. The whole lower mountain is shared with the ridge route; near the 5,700 ft saddle, leave the south ridge and traverse west into the main southwest-face gully and bowl, then climb it to the summit crest. It avoids the 65-degree notch on the old ridge line, and its steepest snow is about 40 degrees. Skiers worked it out as a descent, and with good snow cover it makes the peak a non-technical objective.
overview: The original standard route and the descent line for anything climbed on the north side: nearly 6,000 ft of trailless, sustained, south-facing slope straight up from the North Cascades Highway at Gorge Creek to a 5,720+ ft saddle, then granite slab and a narrow ridge to a broad, heavily corniced summit crest perched on the lip of the northeast wall.

current.approach: There is no trailhead in the usual sense — you step off the highway into the forest. Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of Newhalem near milepost 123, or about the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp turn at the east end of the bridge. There are parking lots at each end; the east lot is signed for motorhomes and oversize vehicles, so park at the west lot. Elevation here is 1,096 ft, and there are accessible restrooms and a short interpretive trail to the Gorge Creek Falls viewpoint. Walk across the bridge to its east end, go a few feet farther east, cross the highway, and pick the easiest place to start uphill into the woods. That is the whole approach: the route and the approach are the same thing from here, 6,000 vertical feet of it. Round trip is about 6.2 miles with roughly 6,000 ft of gain in three miles. Carry water. The slope is south-facing and dry once the snow is gone, and there is no reliable source between the highway and the snowfields high on the mountain. In late spring, snowmelt on the route solves this and simultaneously suppresses the brush, which is why that window is the usual recommendation.
current.descent:
Descend the south ridge crest directly rather than reversing the east-basin variation. The step that drops into the saddle looks formidably steep from camp — steep enough that at least one party detoured around it on the way up — but it is climbed down easily, with all the ledges you need. Below the saddle, retrace your line through Point 5872 and the open slopes.

The work is in the forest. Stay on the line you came up: the cliff bands near 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft need to be turned on the correct side, and getting them wrong means rappelling off trees. Slabs low on the mountain are covered in slippery moss, and one party reported a 3rd-class chimney with an awkward move below it as the crux of the descent. Expect deadfall fields. Total descent time is about 4.1 hours from the summit for a fit party moving well, and every account calls it brutal on the knees.

If you are descending this route after climbing the northeast face, the strong advice from the party that did it is to get the top 1,500 ft done in daylight — that is what lets you avoid the cliff bands — and to carry a compass, because the timber is dense enough to hide the dam lights and a drift to the east puts you in Stetattle Creek.
current.detailed_rack: Very little. One winter party carried no rock protection and no ice screws at all, using occasional ice-axe belays, and was roped for much of the trip above the saddle. For a spring or summer ascent, a light rope, a handful of nuts and a few slings covers the 200 ft of slab above the saddle if it turns out to be bare or wet — nobody has published what that slab actually takes in dry conditions, and the author of that account explicitly asks for that information.
current.pro_needs: Effectively none on the standard line. The protection question is confined to Beckey's 200 ft of slab above the saddle and the short steep step onto the ridge; in snow both are handled with an axe and, at most, an axe belay. Bare-rock beta for that section has never been published. Treat a rope, a few nuts and slings as contingency rather than as a working rack, and be prepared to make the call at the saddle.

name: Deep Blue
beta: Deep Blue begins on a fin-like flake right off the ground — mount the flake and pull a small bulge into easier climbing. Lower/mid pitches include an overhang leading into face climbing to a small ledge below a roof, a pitch through a roof with technical edges to a ledge, and a stretch of 5.11 climbing to a higher ledge below the crux. Higher up, steep 5.10+ lieback flakes lead to an alcove, then a roof with a bouldery V6 crux on perfect edges (~25m pitch), before steep, sequential climbing on good holds leads toward the 5.13c crux pitch itself (~35m, sustained overhanging climbing to a vertical-face crux) and a further 5.12 pitch (~35m) through another roof. The route was developed over several years and finished in 2020; it climbs in 12 pitches with link-up options for parties wanting to move faster, and multiple parties have completed it car-to-car in a day without simul-climbing.
overview: A 12-pitch, fully-bolted 5.13c testpiece on Dolomite Tower's northeast face, starting about 100 ft left of Vanishing Point and climbing steep, technical rock through several roof systems to a 5.13 crux high on the wall.

current.approach: Identical to Vanishing Point's approach from the Barclay Lake Trailhead (see that route) — Barclay Creek Trail to the wash/gully system, fixed-line forested rib, and roped approach slabs to the base of the tower; Deep Blue's start is about 100 ft left of Vanishing Point's first pitch.
approach_variant_names: Barclay Creek Trail, right before the bridge, fixed lines to the tower
current.descent: The usual way down is on foot. From the top, walk off the back side of the tower and cut left into the gully, then traverse around behind Mt. Baring, holding your height rather than dropping, until you meet the main climbers' trail, which leads back to the trailhead. Allow about 2.5-3 hours. The route can also be rappelled on its bolted anchors, but that needs a 70 m rope.
current.detailed_rack: The technical pitches are fully bolted (essentially a big-wall sport route); a single BD cam set from #0.2 to #0.75 plus roughly 16 quickdraws (including 2-4 alpine draws for wandering pitches) covers the route. Cams are needed only on the roped approach pitches below the true start, not on the bolted climbing itself.
current.pro_needs: Almost entirely bolt-protected; the small cam rack exists mainly for the shared roped approach pitches rather than the route proper.

name: North Slopes
beta: From the Alpental base area, ascend barren lower slopes to snowline, then follow the Lower International run and the steep, double-black-diamond Upper International run. From the top of Upper International, a wide ramp leads to a clump of alpine fir below the summit block; a steel cable protects a down-sloping, exposed rock-ledge traverse, followed by a short Class 2-3 scramble to the summit, which carries a radio tower and marker pole. Many parties descend a counterclockwise loop through Edelweiss Bowl and Midway Saddle, glissading Debbie's Gold back to the base.
overview: Denny Mountain rises directly above the Alpental ski area at Snoqualmie Pass, making it one of the most accessible summits in the corridor. Its long, jagged, roughly one-mile ridge runs NNW, with Alpental's ski runs (International, Edelweiss, Armstrong) climbing the peak's eastern flank; this route climbs those same runs and the slopes under the lift lines to the summit ridge. The scramble is little more than a steep grass/talus walk-up for most of its length in summer, but the true highpoint sits atop a short rock step — most parties (Mountaineers trip reports, trailhead logs) describe a brief, exposed Class 2-3 move or narrow ledge/chimney to actually tag the summit, so this isn't a pure Class 2 talus hike start to finish. USGS quad data puts the summit around 5,520+ ft (older NGVD29 datum); some newer survey accounts list it closer to 5,614-5,620 ft.

current.approach: Park at the large Alpental Ski Area lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 1.4 miles/2 miles up from I-90 Exit 52, per differing trip-report odometers), elevation roughly 3,100 ft. There is no signed trailhead or maintained trail for Denny Mountain itself — climbers cross the base area and pick up boot-track/climber's paths under the old Armstrong Express / Sessel chairline on the mountain's north-facing slopes. Early season or in a lingering snowpack this is straightforward: hike the barren lower ski slopes for a few hundred feet of gain to snowline, then switch to crampons/axe and follow the Lower International ski run up into a small basin. From there the route continues up the steep Upper International run (a double-black-diamond pitch that holds firm snow late into the year and is the crux of the ascent in spring conditions) to the top of the Edelweiss chairlift unloading station (the Edelweiss lift was rebuilt as a new Doppelmayr triple chair, opened January 2026, replacing the original 1967 Riblet double that had earned it the old 'Edelweiss' nickname on this route). In summer/dry conditions the same line goes as a rough boot-path and talus/scree scramble through brush, small hemlocks, and huckleberry — expect neck-deep slide alder and bramble in spots, loose scree underfoot, and only intermittent pink/white/blue flagging that does not reliably mark the line; route-finding is the main hazard low on the mountain. Above the lift station, angle up the wide open ramp toward the summit horn; this transitions from scree/heather to broken rock. A fixed steel cable (a short via-ferrata-style handline) protects an exposed, down-sloping and often slick rock ledge traverse just below the top. The route finishes with a short Class 2–3 scramble (some parties note a stiffer Class 3–4 move) through a narrow rock cleft to the summit block, which carries an old radio-relay structure and a survey marker. One-way distance/gain from the lot to the summit runs roughly 2.3–2.4 miles and about 2,500 ft, consistent with the ~4.7 mi (7.56 km) round-trip logged for this route; best window is late spring through mid-July after the resort closes but before the snow gullies melt out and expose looser rock and scree.
approach_variant_names: Alpental base area and the ski runs under the old Armstrong Express line
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or typically used on the standard North Slopes route. Reverse the summit cleft and cable-protected ledge back down to the top of the Edelweiss lift station (rebuilt as a new triple chair in January 2026), taking care on the down-sloping ledge traverse (it is more exposure-sensitive descending than ascending). From there, most parties drop into Edelweiss Bowl rather than exactly retracing the International runs: descend the open bowl, cross east through Midway Saddle, and finish down Debbie's Gold ski run back to the base area, glissading or boot-skiing the snow where conditions allow — this is faster than downclimbing the steep Upper International pitch and is the descent line most parties use (roughly 1.3 hours down versus 2.5–2.7 hours up). In low-snow/summer conditions without a glissade path, simply reverse the ascent line of least resistance back through the ski-slope brush and scree to the base lodge, watching for loose rock and the same route-finding ambiguity encountered on the way up. Hazards on descent are exposure on the cable ledge, potential glissade-path hazards (rocks, run-out onto talus) in Edelweiss Bowl, and loose/scree footing lower down; no technical rope work is needed on this route.
current.detailed_rack: Not a roped climb for most parties; some parties carry a short sling/handline as backup on the cable-protected ledge below the summit.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection beyond the resort-installed steel cable on the final ledge; a rope is not typically used but could be carried for extra security on that section.
current.rope_note: Class 3 scramble typically approached via Alpental ski area/Source Lake; ice axe and helmet required per Mountaineers guidance, microspikes/crampons recommended if snow is firm.

name: Southeast Ridge
beta: From Bird Creek Camp (~4,200 ft) on the Devore Creek Trail, traverse to open meadows and a waterfall cirque, then climb semi-open slopes and snow ramps into the ~7,000 ft basin between Wy'North Peak and Devore Peak (the Bird Lakes basin). Cross Bird Creek at the northern lake and hike southeast up talus/scree to a col at roughly 7,500 ft on Devore's southeast ridge. From the col, scramble west along Class 3 terrain, working past a false summit block, to an unavoidable ~20-ft rock step (Class 5.0-5.4) just below the true summit; a short final Class 3-4 pitch tops out at the 1940 first-ascent register.
overview: Devore Peak (8,382 ft) is the high point of a long, remote north-south ridge in the Glacier Peak Wilderness dividing Company and Hilgard Creeks (west) from Devore Creek (east), about 6 miles WSW of Stehekin on Lake Chelan. It is composed of granodiorite and is one of Washington's Bulger '100 Highest Peaks.' The standard line climbs the peak's southeast ridge/face from the Bird Creek basin above Devore Creek — a broad talus and rock scramble broken by one short, exposed crux move on the true summit block. It was first climbed July 28, 1940 by Everett and Ida Darr, Abigail and Stuart Avery, Jane Foster and Grant McConnell, and Paul Parker; their original summit register has since been recovered intact by later climbers.

current.approach: Devore Peak is only reachable by a multi-day approach out of Stehekin, at the head of Lake Chelan — there is no road access. Drive to Fields Point Landing (or Chelan) and take the Lady of the Lake II or Lady Express passenger ferry up-lake to Stehekin (roughly a 2-4 hour boat ride depending on which boat); the National Park Service shuttle bus or a short water-taxi hop then covers the last few miles to Weaver Point Campground on the north shore, which is the trailhead (some parties instead bike or hike the road from Stehekin to High Bridge/Harlequin Bridge and pick up the Stehekin River Trail on foot). From Weaver Point (~1,160 ft), pick up the Devore Creek Trail (USFS Trail #1244). The trail switchbacks steeply — roughly 30 switchbacks over about 2 miles — up through open forest to the Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary at ~2,300 ft, then settles into a steady, unrelenting climb alongside Devore Creek for another 3+ miles; this middle section sees little maintenance and can be brushy underfoot. Devore Creek is crossed/paralleled repeatedly and is the reliable water source through this stretch. At roughly 4-5 miles from Weaver Point you reach Bird Creek Camp (~4,200 ft), the last established campsite and a common bivy for a two-day itinerary. From here leave the maintained tread and follow the open-forest use path/animal trails up along Bird Creek about another mile to a higher, unofficial camp at ~5,400 ft — many parties who want a single big summit day push to this basin instead. Continue upvalley along Bird Creek through heather benches and a talus staircase into a broader open basin holding the Bird Lakes (~7,000 ft); cross Bird Creek near the northern lake (last reliable water before the summit ridge). From the lake basin, climb loose Class 2-3 talus/scree southeast to a col (~7,500 ft) on Devore's southeast ridge, passing beneath a pair of distinctive rock towers locally called "the Bottles." Expect lingering snow in this basin and on the col approach well into July, sometimes requiring an ice axe/crampons on a short ~40-degree traverse; loose rock and occasional avalanche debris are the main hazards on this upper section. From the col, the route turns west along the summit ridge/west flank — ledges and shallow gullies of variable rock quality (some solid, some "kitty-litter"-covered slab) lead through Class 3-4 scrambling with a route-finding crux threading the ledge systems below the summit block.
approach_variant_names: Devore Creek Trail and the Bird Creek basin
current.descent: Descend the same way you came up: reverse the west-ridge/west-flank ledge system back down to the 7,500 ft col, then drop into the Bird Lakes basin and follow Bird Creek back down through the 5,400 ft high camp to Bird Creek Camp and the maintained Devore Creek Trail to Weaver Point. This is fundamentally a downclimb, not a rappel-dependent descent — most of the Class 3-4 terrain is downclimbed in place. The one spot that regularly gets a rope is a short, steep ~20-ft 4th-class rock step just below the summit; there are no bolts or chains, but slung webbing rappel anchors have been found in place at the edge of the summit ridge and above the step — inspect and back up any old webbing before trusting it (carry spare cord), or downclimb it with a spot/handline. At least one party describes placing two short rappels on the descent (the summit step plus one more short step lower on the ridge where a loaded pack makes downclimbing feel insecure); a single 30m rope, or a doubled 60m rope, is more than enough length for either. Treat this as an optional-rappel route: confident scramblers downclimb the whole thing with zero rappels, while parties less comfortable with exposed 4th class commonly place one or two short raps off natural anchors. The bigger real hazard on descent is footing — the ridge and the approach basin are loose talus, scree, and "kitty-litter" over slab, and at least one climber has taken a ~15-ft scree fall here with contusions and a bruised rib, so move carefully, spread the party out to avoid rockfall onto those below, and expect the ~7,200 ft of elevation loss back to Weaver Point (and the ferry schedule back down Lake Chelan) to be a long day.
current.detailed_rack: Most parties solo the short 5.0-5.4 crux, but a single rope and a small rack (a few nuts/small cams plus slings) let you belay, protect, or rappel the ~20-ft rock step; a sling around a nearby tree/horn has served as an anchor for past parties. No additional technical gear is needed for the Class 2-4 talus, gully, and ridge terrain below or above it.
rack: 30-60m rope for the exposed crux/optional rappel
current.pro_needs: A light rock rack (a few small-to-mid cams and nuts) plus a 30-60m rope is worth carrying for the short, exposed low-5th-class crux move and optional rappel near the true summit; unnecessary for the rest of the Class 3-4 scramble.
bivy: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
current.rope_note: Approach to a col (~7,500 ft) on Devore's SE ridge, then face scramble to summit with routefinding; Mountaineers beta describes Class 4 terrain with a few Class 5 moves, and descent uses a mix of rappels and downclimbing — meaningfully harder than the listed Class 2-3 grade.

name: Direct Southwest Buttress
beta: 8-pitch, III 5.10a alpine rock route on Dorado Needle's southwest buttress, sharing the standard Southwest Buttress approach and lower gully but taking a steeper, more sustained direct start.
overview: A harder, more direct variation of the Southwest Buttress, established by Mike Preiss and Mark Bunker in September 2006. Rather than following the standard line's easier ramps, it stays on the direct crest of the buttress for sustained 5.9-5.10 climbing on generally good granite, sharing the same approach and much of the same descent as the standard Southwest Buttress.

current.approach: Shares the standard Southwest Buttress's approach and the broader Eldorado-area approach: from the Cascade River Road trailhead (~2,100 ft), cross the Cascade River and climb the climbers' path through forest and talus into Eldorado/Roush Creek Basin, then up to an Inspiration Glacier-area high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft (~5.8 mi, ~5,500 ft gain from the car). From camp, cross the Inspiration Glacier to the Inspiration-McAllister col, descend onto the McAllister Glacier (best passage on its skier's right side near steeper crevassed sections), and ascend the prominent gully — often snow-filled year-round — that runs from about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McAllister pass up to the base of the buttress; a rope-up may be needed here as a moat guarding the base of the climb can present an exposed, deep gap. Where the Direct start diverges from the standard 1985 line: instead of traversing right partway up the approach gully/lower buttress, continue straight up ("strait up" per the route description) from the same gully entry point onto two direct-start pitches of 4th/low-5th scrambling leading to three vertical cracks; the rightmost of these is climbed at 5.8-ish through the crux to a large bench, after which an awkward 5.8+ section and blocky mid-5th rock rejoin the standard 1985 route for the remaining pitches to the summit ridge.
approach_variant_names: Same gully as the standard buttress — the difference is one turn at its top
current.descent: The Direct start rejoins the standard Southwest Buttress after its first two pitches, so the descent is the same as the standard route's: from the top, return to the head of the approach gully and make a single-rope rappel (climbers may need to downclimb or work around an open moat at the bottom). Alternatively, from a large rock on the ridge about 10 meters north of the true summit, a fixed rappel ring and sling anchor lets you make a double-rope (two-strand) rappel down to a steep snow section that still connects to rock, avoiding a direct moat crossing via a snow bridge that has historically stayed solid there. From the bottom of either rappel, descend the glacier back down to the notch/col where you left the McAllister Glacier on approach, then reverse the glacier crossing back to high camp. Because this is a mixed rock/snow/glacier descent with an in-situ ring anchor plus natural gully rappel stations, carry standard rappel backup material (a few slings/cord) in case fixed gear needs supplementing, and reassess the moat/snow-bridge crossing each trip since it is snow-condition dependent and can deteriorate later in the season.
current.detailed_rack: Bring the standard Southwest Buttress rack (single set to #3 Camalot with doubles in 0.5, 0.75, 1, plus nuts) and supplement with additional thin cams and mid-to-large cams (3"+); small cams provide good protection/anchoring on the pillar section.
current.pro_needs: Thin-to-mid gear is needed through the crack pitch; small cams back up natural anchor options on the pillar.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
current.rope_note: Grade III+ alpine rock buttress, ~13 pitches over 1000+ ft; standard Southwest Buttress line is 5.7-5.8 (first pitch a full 55-57m rope length), the 'Direct' variant follows a steeper/harder line to reach 5.10a. Glacier approach via Marble Creek-McAllister Pass gully (year-round snow to 35 deg) requires ice axe/crampons.

name: The Dirty
beta: Multi-pitch alpine rock route with run-out sections requiring careful route-finding. Loose rock throughout with minimal protection on upper pitches, particularly the exposed Jenga Traverse on the final pitch. The route starts on the second obvious rib and is mostly gear-protected, with two bolted pitches (the second and sixth) and gear climbing through corners.
overview: A 700-foot, 7-pitch alpine rock climb on the south wall featuring loose chossy rock and the famous Jenga Traverse knife-edge crossing. The route deteriorates in rock quality mid-way but remains a classic Tieton alpine experience.

current.approach: From Naches, take US-12 west roughly 23 miles to just past the Rimrock Lake Dam, then turn south onto Tieton Reservoir Road (FR-1200). For the popular rock routes on the eastern cliffs, park in one of the pullouts along Tieton Road near a spring marked by a split-rail fence and follow the steep climbers' trail uphill to the base of the routes. To reach the summit via the non-technical Southwest Ridge, continue on FR-1200 to the South Fork/campground turnoff, park near the restroom area, and hike cross-country, following criss-crossing boot-paths while staying on the ridge crest until it becomes an established path to the summit block. The area melts out quickly and is climbable from May through November.
approach_variant_names: Tieton Road spring, climbers' trail, then left along the base
current.descent: Descend via the rocky gully to climber's right, with one rappel required midway. Alternatively, descend via the Gangsta Rap descent route toward Rimrock Lake. Multiple rappel anchors exist; bring adequate rope for the descent.
current.detailed_rack: Carabiners and draws for bolted sections; cams to 3 inches and nuts for crack sections. Bring slings for anchors and protection. Quick draws recommended for the bolted pitches.
current.pro_needs: Carry gear to 3 inches and a dozen draws. Traditional protection with bolted anchors on initial pitches, transitioning to natural protection and minimal bolting higher on the route.
current.rope_note: Two separate 60m ropes are commonly used on this route (useful for rappel descent options), though a single 60m rope with the walk-off is also viable.

name: Django
beta: P1 climbs left past several bolts (pinch a peanut-shaped hold and step up and right into a dish); the crux reaches right up a buttress-like feature past more bolts to chains. P2 is a shorter ~50 ft 5.10 pitch above the belay to a ledge with more chains.
overview: The best-regarded line at Summertime Crag: a technical, reachy bolted face pitch on the far-left side of the cliff, followed by a short 5.10 second pitch to a ledge.

current.approach: Summertime Crag uses a different trailhead than the other four areas' shared Blue Lake approach. From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 through Mazama toward Washington Pass (or, coming from Seattle, continue past Washington Pass toward Mazama on SR-20); park at a small pullout on the east side of the highway, just before the larger 'Spires Gully' parking area used to access the Early Winters Spires from the east. From the pullout, descend off the road down through trees, cross Early Winters Creek, follow it briefly downstream, then climb up-slope and contour left to reach the crag — about a 20-25 minute walk with minimal elevation change. The crag stays shaded until mid-afternoon in summer, making it a popular warm-weather alternative when Mazama-area cragging runs hot.
current.descent: From either belay/anchor, lower or make a single-rope rappel back to the base of the route; reverse the approach (descend to the creek, cross, climb back up to the road) to return to the car.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted sport line; bring 12-14 quickdraws and a 60m rope (70m gives more lowering margin).
current.pro_needs: No trad gear required — bolts only.

name: Dome Glacier
beta: This classic 3-4 day alpine climb involves a long backpack approach followed by technical glacier travel and exposed rock scrambling on the famous Cheval crux. The route is best suited for experienced mountaineers comfortable with crevasse rescue, glacier navigation, and exposed Class 4-5 rock.
overview: Dome Peak is the glaciated centerpiece and customary high point of the famed Ptarmigan Traverse, crowning a sea of ice deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. Its broad summit rewards climbers with one of the great panoramas of the North Cascades.

current.approach: From the Downey Creek Campground trailhead (~1,450 ft) on Suiattle River Road (FR 26), take the Downey Creek Trail #768, staying on the east bank of Downey Creek through old-growth forest. The trail is rough and lightly maintained — expect brush, downed timber, and washed-out sections; a footlog or ford may be needed at Bachelor Creek (~6.5 mi in), which has been scoured by past avalanches that swept debris across the valley and buried sections of trail. Beyond Bachelor Creek the trail climbs steeply out of the valley toward Cub Lake, gaining roughly 4,000+ ft from the trailhead; this stretch crosses open avalanche paths below Spire Point that should be assessed for stability in early-season snow. Camp is typically made in meadows southeast of Cub Lake (~5,300 ft) or, better positioned for summit day, up on the ridge above at ~6,200 ft (add ~1 hr from the lake). Reported car-to-camp time is 9-11 hours given the distance, brush, and elevation gain — budget this as a genuine multi-day approach, not a day hike-in. From high camp, a boot path crosses the south ridge toward Spire Point, then the route drops ~200 ft and traverses cross-country (roughly 80° bearing) below cliff bands, over glacier-polished slabs (bare rock in late season, snow-covered early season) and a boulder/snow slope, to gain the base of the Dome Glacier. This traverse is unmarked route-finding on exposed, sometimes loose terrain — a map/compass or GPS track is strongly recommended.
approach_variant_names: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the rock arête (~500 ft) back to the notch at 8,560 ft, then down the snow slope (~300 ft) onto the Dome Glacier, and back down-glacier along the ascent track to the base of the climb, retracing the cross-country traverse back to high camp. The rock arête itself is narrow, exposed, and largely featureless — many parties belay or fix a handline/rappel for at least part of it rather than downclimbing unroped, especially in the upper section near the summit. The more consequential technical step is typically the bergschrund on the Dome Glacier below the notch: depending on the season and how open the 'schrund is, parties commonly need one rappel (single 60m rope reported sufficient) to get down past it safely, building an anchor from snow pickets, a buried deadman, or a v-thread in firm ice — there are no fixed/bolted anchors on this remote, seldom-traveled route. In a low-snow year or if the bergschrund is well-bridged, this step may be downclimbable with no rappel at all, so treat the rappel as conditions-dependent rather than fixed. Below the glacier, re-cross the loose/polished traverse back toward Cub Lake camp with care, then descend the Downey Creek Trail back to the trailhead, watching again for the avalanche-debris and washout sections near Bachelor Creek.
current.detailed_rack: Standard glacier kit (2-3 pickets or ice screws) plus a light rock rack for the summit ridge: a few slings and optionally one small cam or nut in the 0.5in range -- most parties climb this short section unroped or with a quick simul-pitch.
current.pro_needs: Minimal rock protection -- this is glacier travel with a short unroped or simul-climbed scramble finish, not a pitched rock climb; bring slings more than cams.

name: Doorway Flake
beta: Pitch 1 (5.8) climbs sculpted knobs to a hanging flake with stemming and crack moves. Pitch 2 (5.9) is the crux — bolt-protected face climbing. Pitch 3 (5.7) follows a clean crack system, and pitches 4-5 (5.6) ease through dihedrals and slab to the top.
overview: A 5-pitch, 700-ft route on the Far Western Wall reaching a distinctive hanging flake, with sculpted-knob face climbing low down and a bolt-protected 5.9 face crux on pitch two.

current.approach: South Face is another wall within the same Squire Creek Walls complex as Waterfall Basin, reached from the same Darrington trailhead: I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. From there, walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing to the Squire Creek Trail sign and on to two cut logs with old logging cable, turn right onto the boot track, ford Squire Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest up two gullies to the grassy saddle below the South Face, roughly 3 hours from the car. For Doorway Flake, go west along the base of the wall past the start of Skeena26 and scramble 4th class onto the far western wall.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
current.descent: Rappel the line of ascent using the fixed hand-drilled bolt and Fixe chain anchors; two 60m ropes recommended.
current.detailed_rack: Single standard rack to 4 inches, about a dozen quickdraws (plus a few longer/extended ones), and two 60m ropes for the rappel descent.
current.pro_needs: Bolt protection on the pitch-2 face crux, with gear placements in the flake, crack, and dihedral sections on the remaining pitches; all bolts are hand-drilled per Wilderness rules.
bivy: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac

name: East Ridge / Inspiration Glacier
beta: From the Eldorado East Ridge high camp (~7,400 ft), rope up and cross the Inspiration and McAllister Glaciers to the col between Pt. 8386 and Dorado Needle. The route starts with a loose, thinly-protected 5.5 pitch off the col, eases into several ropelengths of class 3-4 ridge terrain (with a glacier traverse and moat crossing to regain the ridge partway up), then several ropelengths of 3rd-to-low-5th-class climbing to a sub-summit tower. Two short rappels drop into a notch below the true summit, followed by two sustained, high-quality 5.7 pitches to the top. Most parties take 8-12 hours round trip from high camp to summit and back, descending via the technical Northwest Ridge.
overview: A moderate, remote alpine rock ridge climb on a striking granite spire in the heart of the Eldorado Ice Cap, reached by crossing the Inspiration and McAllister Glaciers from an Eldorado East Ridge high camp, then finishing on two pitches of clean 5.7 crack climbing to the summit.

current.approach: Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount about 20 miles to the Eldorado Trailhead (~2,100 ft; first 10 miles paved, remainder rough gravel, high-clearance recommended). Hike the Eldorado Trail through forest, cross a creek, and climb steeply to the Eldorado Glacier, then follow the East Ridge of Eldorado Peak to a high camp around 7,400 ft (roughly 4 miles and ~6,000 ft of gain). From camp, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier to reach the col at the base of Dorado Needle's East Ridge.
approach_variant_names: Inspiration and McAllister to the col between Point 8386 and the Needle
current.descent: From the summit, avoid old/misleading rappel tat and head toward the Northwest Ridge. Locate a wrapped-block rappel anchor a short distance above a stance; rappel roughly 30m (100 ft) to another stance, then scramble easy ledges to a further, uncomplicated rappel that lands in a moatless notch. From there, navigate steep crevasses on climber's right to regain the McAllister-Inspiration col and the glacier route back to camp.
current.detailed_rack: A single rack of cams to 3 inches (e.g. doubles from 0.5-2 with a 3 and small tricams) and a single 60m rope covers the technical pitches.
current.pro_needs: Protection is thin and sometimes suspect on the lower 5.5 pitch off the col — test every placement to ensure it's attached to the mountain; gear improves and cracks are better higher up on the two 5.7 pitches near the summit.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Dot Mountain is almost never climbed as a standalone objective — it is reached via a multi-day wilderness backpack, typically combined with Ptarmigan Peak, Tatoosh Buttes, and/or Mount Lago. From a high camp on Tamarack Ridge or near Dot Lakes, parties gain the Ptarmigan-Dot saddle and walk up talus/scree to the summit; the descent (or an alternate ascent) can be made via the south ridge, which stays Class 3 but has real exposure on its narrow, blocky crest.
overview: Dot Mountain (~8,220–8,225 ft) is a minor summit on the ridge running north from Mount Lago to Ptarmigan Peak in the remote central Pasayten Wilderness, about a mile south of Ptarmigan — not in the Carru/Osceola cluster proper, though the Lago-Carru col is the usual approach line. It's named for Dot (Adele) Wernstedt, wife of Lage Wernstedt, the USFS topographer/climber who mapped much of the Pasayten and made many first ascents there in the 1920s. With modest independent prominence, Dot is a Class 3 ridge scramble (the summit itself an easy talus walk-up) almost always tagged onto a Lago-Carru-Ptarmigan traverse or a broader Pasayten Bulger-bagging trip, and sits near what hikers have called the most remote point in the entire Pasayten Wilderness.

current.approach: From the Slate Pass trailhead (~6,900', reached via the Harts Pass Road — one of the highest drivable roads in Washington), pick up the Buckskin Ridge Trail #498 heading north/northeast into the Pasayten Wilderness. About 0.5 mile in, a cutoff splits off toward the Robinson Creek–Middle Fork Trail #478; parties bound for Dot Mountain generally follow the Eureka Creek drainage (reached by following the Middle Fork Pasayten trail down-valley, then climbing over Freds Pass into the head of Eureka Creek Basin) rather than staying on the full Buckskin Ridge crest toward Silver/Buckskin Lakes. The trail through Eureka Creek Basin runs through open, wildflower-strewn meadows (avalanche lilies in early/mid season) with larch groves higher up, and this is the last reliable running water for the day — carry what you'll need above it. From the basin, leave the trail and climb off-trail east/southeast to the Lago–Carru col on the ridge between Mount Carru and Mount Lago. From the col, contour Mount Lago's rocky, talus-covered north slopes (loose 6–12" rock; a helmet is worth carrying for rockfall) down to a small tarn near 7,400', which is the standard overnight camp given the ~35–36 mile round-trip distance. From the tarn/col, regain the crest and follow it north: the first real obstacle is Point 8207, the technical crux of the traverse (exposed class 3–4 scrambling on otherwise solid rock), followed by Point 8165 with sustained class 3 moves and one exposed, improbable-looking ledge traverse through a small cliff band — most parties bypass Pt 8165's true summit to the west. Beyond that the ridge relents into a pleasant, mostly-dirt walk above treeline, and Dot Mountain's summit is reached by an easy, non-technical walk-up along the crest. Note there is no water anywhere on this high ridge traverse until a small tarn on Ptarmigan Peak's south shoulder, well beyond Dot Mountain.
approach_variant_names: The Lago-Carru col and the ridge crest north
current.descent: This is an off-trail ridge scramble with no fixed hardware and no rappelling anywhere on it — rappels: 0. The way down is to reverse the ascent line. From Dot Mountain, retrace the ridge crest south, re-negotiating the exposed ledge traverse and class 3 moves on Point 8165 and the class 3–4 crux on Point 8207; both are more awkward downclimbing than climbing, so face in where needed and watch for loose blocks near the crux. Regain the Lago–Carru col and reverse the contour across Mount Lago's loose north-slope talus back down to the 7,400' tarn — parties describe this specific slope as a grinding, ankle-turning scree/talus descent, easier going up than down, so take it slow. From the tarn, drop back into Eureka Creek Basin and climb back over Freds Pass and follow the Middle Fork Pasayten trail up-valley for the long return to the Slate Pass trailhead. Given the total distance (~35–36 miles round trip) and elevation swing, this route is normally done as a multi-day trip with a high camp near the Lago–Carru col rather than a single push — so for most parties the 'descent' off Dot Mountain is really the return leg to that high camp, with the longer trail descent to the car following on a subsequent day. No rope, harness, or rappel device is needed anywhere on this route; a helmet for the loose ridge and talus sections is the main safety item worth carrying.
current.pro_needs: Class 3 talus/ridge scramble, with one short Class 4 step on Point 8207 that can be skirted on its north side. No rope or technical protection normally needed.
bivy: 7,400 ft Tarn Camp, Mount Lago north side
Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
current.rope_note: Class 3 ridge scramble on talus and rock, with one short Class 4 step on Point 8207 that can be skirted on its north side; no rope or rack needed, ice axe only if early-season snow persists.

name: Serpentine Arête
beta: Climbs an obvious dihedral system past two trees with webbing to a large terrace, then crack systems and a small dihedral to the crux — two consecutive 5.8 pitches (a finger crack into a splitter hand crack, then a dihedral with bomber finger locks) that can be linked with a 70m rope. Above the crux the route stays on the ridge crest with mostly 3rd-4th class/low-5th scrambling, a short downclimb, and a sandy gully to the summit area. All of the technical climbing is on solid rock even though the low-5th-class sections are loose.
overview: A long, high-quality granite line up the right (west) side of Dragontail's north face, roughly 200 ft right of Backbone Ridge, following corners and crack systems to two sustained 5.8 crux pitches before ridge scrambling to the summit.

current.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail ~4 mi / 2,280 ft gain to Colchuck Lake (5,574 ft). Round the lake's west shore to its south end, boulder-hop onto the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine, and traverse it toward the orange-colored rock marking the route start; 4th-class ledges lead up to a snow finger and the base of the technical climbing. Roughly 3 hours car-to-base at a brisk pace.
approach_variant_names: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
current.descent: From the summit, most parties head down the loose sandy gully shared with the top of Backbone Ridge, boot-ski or downclimb the upper Snow Creek Glacier snowfield where present, then traverse to Aasgard Pass (7,841 ft) and descend its steep, loose talus/scree back to Colchuck Lake. Crampons and an ice axe are important for this descent whenever snow/ice remain on the upper mountain or in Aasgard Pass. Some parties instead reverse via Colchuck Glacier/Col — route-find carefully, as the descent gully is loose and cliffs out if the wrong line is taken.
current.detailed_rack: Standard rack to 3 inches with doubles through the smaller-to-mid sizes for the crack systems; the crux pitches take good, solid gear.
current.pro_needs: Gear to 3 inches is sufficient; no wide gear required. Long runners help manage rope drag on the wandering ridge pitches.
bivy: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side

name: Drew's Magical Wonderland
beta: Easy jugs with close bolts, making it an accessible, confidence-building climb for developing climbers.
overview: An easy, closely-bolted beginner-friendly pitch on a small, remote NE-facing cliff band at the far end of the East Face.

current.approach: Descend into the talus field below Nocturnal Pulse for about 200 ft, passing The Meeperland Empire; continue uphill on the climbers' right side of Meeperland until reaching a steep wall with abandoned projects; walk beneath this wall until spotting Project Crack, then traverse through the talus field to the far end of the small NE-facing cliff band.
current.descent: Single lower from the top; short route within any standard rope length.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted with closely-spaced bolts: 5 bolts to a chain anchor.
current.pro_needs: Short sport rack of 5 quickdraws; well-protected given close bolt spacing.

name: Drilling Me Softly
beta: Fully bolted 5.10b/c sport pitch on Sofa King Buttress, positioned as the leftmost route on the wall. The line (FA party Wylie Moreshead) is known for the sheer variety of technique packed into one pitch rather than a single hard crux — 3D stemming, backstepping, flagging, a roof, laybacking, jugs, crimps and underclings. Protected by 12 bolts to chain anchors at the top; photos of the route show the crux section and a rest stance before an upper bulge.
overview: Alpine sport climb at Sofa King Buttress in The Citidel area.

current.approach: From I-90 Exit 54 (Hyak), follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, continuing past where the pavement ends to the junction at Ollallie Meadow where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.
current.descent: Single-pitch, fully bolted sport route with a chain lower-off anchor at the top; there is no walk-off. Clip/thread the chains and lower back to the base.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted: 12 bolts to a two-bolt chain anchor. No trad gear needed.
current.pro_needs: Sport rack only — 12 quickdraws (plus 1-2 extra for the anchor). No natural/trad protection required or possible.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route; one single rope lowers off the chain anchor.
